In the proposal/initiation phase (起案フェーズ), the final required deliverable is the proposal document (企画書). Creating it involves organizing various information, making the proposal idea concrete, and connecting it to project launch.
Proposal document (企画書) formats are often predefined by companies using internal systems or Excel templates.
The proposal creation process should be understood; Chapter 5 explains the required inputs along the following items and process steps.
Key process steps for building the proposal: ① 施策検討 (measure/policy consideration), ② 業務検討 (business consideration), ③ システム検討 (system consideration), ④ プロジェクト計画 (project planning).

Required inputs for the proposal (企画書に必要なインプット) include: 起案部門 (proposing department), 課題一覧 (list of issues), As-Is 業務フロー (current-state business flow), 解決する課題特定 (identification of issues to solve), 業務取り組み概要 (overview of business initiatives), To-Be 業務フロー (future-state business flow), システム要求 (system requirements), システム外費用 (non-system costs), 想定効果 (expected effects/benefits), プロジェクトマイルストーン (project milestones), 体制 (organization/staffing), システム概要 (system overview), システム費用 (system costs), and 社内SE (internal systems engineer).
The proposal document is the final artifact that consolidates these inputs from business, system, and project-planning perspectives.
The proposing department (起案部門), not the internal SE (社内SE), is the party responsible for creating the project proposal document (企画書).

When a business department approaches an internal SE requesting introduction of a specific system, they often skip defining the true project purpose so that systemization itself becomes the goal rather than a means; this must be avoided.

Systemization should not be considered until the proposing department has prepared; proceeding without the proposer’s own analysis makes the purpose of the system unclear and puts the cart before the horse (本末転倒).
Standard planning sequence: (1) Consider measures — collect issues from As-Is business flows or existing services and identify those that must be solved according to corporate strategy.

Standard planning sequence: (2) Advance business consideration — design To-Be business flows, derive and organize system requirements, estimate non-system budgets, and quantify expected benefits of resolving the issues.
Standard planning sequence: (3) Consider systemization — determine how the system will solve the identified issues, ensuring alignment with the IT department’s strategy and roadmap.

Standard planning sequence: (4) Create the project plan — only after both the proposing department’s and the internal SE’s analyses have matured should the required organization/structure and high-level milestones be decided.
Deciding organization and milestones before deciding what the project will actually do commonly produces resource shortages or unrealistic plans.
As-Is/To-Be業務フローは業務の流れを図式化したものであり、As-Is業務フローは現在の業務を可視化した図、To-Be業務フローは未来の想定業務を可視化した図である。
業務フローは、業務改善ポイントの洗い出し、未来の想定業務の検討、ユーザートレーニング時の机上説明などに使用される。
起案フェーズでは、To-Be業務フローからどの業務プロセス部分をシステム化して改善できるかを検討する。
As-Is/To-Be業務フローの作成主体は基本的に業務ユーザーであり、社内SEは業務部門の作成を支援する役割を担う。
よくある失敗として、社内SEが業務フローを作成して責任まで負わされるケースや、起案フェーズからいきなり詳細化して全体感を押さえられないケースがある。
誰が・いつ・どの粒度まで業務フローを準備するかを事前に決める必要がある。
業務フローには粒度が存在し、起案フェーズ・立ち上げフェーズ・構築フェーズそれぞれで成果物が登場し、プロジェクト進行に伴い詳細化・掘り下げていく。
起案フェーズではハイレベル（抽象度の高い）業務フローを検討し、立ち上げフェーズで詳細化を進め、構築フェーズでさらに詳細まで落とし込む。
前工程での検討が甘いと、後工程で粒度の粗い業務フローをベースに詳細化しなければならなくなる。

In the project proposal (起案) phase, high-level As-Is/To-Be business process flows (業務フロー) should be created; if the proposer proceeds without documenting them, the internal SE should prompt documentation as soon as noticed.

The business department owns business-flow creation and remains responsible for it; the internal SE acts only as a support role and may create a draft or assist when that helps the project move smoothly.
Reuse existing in-house business-flow documents: match notation, legends, and style so later sharing and maintenance are easier.

Have business users produce one sample flow early and review it; capability cannot be judged from writing rules alone. If they cannot write flows at all, reconsider the overall timeline or ask a manager whether an internal training group exists.
Business-flow detailing is performed across phases (proposal/起案, launch/立ち上げ, construction/構築); the proposal phase focuses on high-level As-Is/To-Be views rather than detailed notation.
ITソリューション検討とは、業務ユーザーの要求に基づき、課題をどのようにITで解消できるか（How）を検討することである。
ITソリューション検討は、システム要求、プロジェクトの目的、IT戦略、ITロードマップ、既存システムランドスケープなどのポイントを加味して行う必要がある。
業務ユーザーが「XXXシステムがほしい！」などと要求してくる場合があるが、これは間違った要求である。システムの提案は社内SEが行う。
社内SEは、ユーザーのどんな課題を解決するための要求なのかを確認する必要がある。
ITソリューション検討の確認ポイント：どのような課題を解決しようとしているか／要求が本来の目的にそっているか／IT戦略やITロードマップとの整合性は／提案するシステムは既存のシステムランドスケープと整合するか。
検討にはシステム構築の選択肢の提案も含まれる（図5-5 ITソリューション検討のポイント）。
When making a project proposal, evaluate options using business merits/demerits, system merits/demerits, approximate 5-year total investment cost, and expected delivery time (納期).

Project purpose must be understood in parallel with requirements: DX, BPR and other improvement methods change the scope of possible measures; confirm that the project's aim is consistent with the understood requirements.

Never propose a system based only on received requirements. Proposals must pursue overall (not partial) optimization and therefore require understanding of the organization's IT strategy and IT roadmap.

Example of strategy alignment: if corporate policy is moving to the cloud, an on-premises solution that technically meets the stated requirements still requires careful scrutiny of whether it is truly the right answer.

Designing a new system solely from the current request produces siloed systems. After receiving requirements, check consistency with the existing system landscape; better alignment simplifies operations and suppresses cost.

A typical proposal table compares four options: (1) modify existing system (small business change, but aging will force migration in X years), (2) introduce a package (large business change + standardization, package selection required), (3) use SaaS (large business change + standardization, possible integrated operations with other domains), (4) RPA (covers only ~50 % of business requirements). Each row shows corresponding system implications, 5-year cost and lead time.
IT departments should propose which solution is most appropriate; what is prioritized determines the system's overall direction.

Focus on mechanisms that contribute to the business: systems that support repetitive work performed by many people, not merely 'scratch-an-itch' tools for specific users or tasks. Niche tools are not always bad if they show cost-effectiveness and fit the IT strategy/roadmap, but they are not the main path.
First-year in-house SEs participating in IT solution discussions often fall into local (individual) optimization; they must be careful to avoid this.

Business companies tend to produce locally optimized or siloed systems because of their structure: business units often have more discretion and voice than IT, and those units are themselves fragmented domestically and internationally.
In-house SEs must understand this silo-prone structure and ask whether a business-unit request has already been addressed elsewhere or can be integrated with other departments.
Siloed construction: each business unit (and overseas units) builds its own systems independently (e.g., systems A–E for units A–E).
Desired approach: integrate initiatives across units (domestic and overseas) into a shared IT platform rather than separate systems.
Same-company similar business models and processes should be candidates for integration rather than duplicated systems.
From a systems-support viewpoint, requirements can often be integrated rather than spawning isolated solutions; this is a core way to prevent siloing (サイロ化).
Check IT strategy and IT roadmap: extend the time horizon into the future and confirm the direction the organization as a whole is heading before proposing a new system.
Check whether existing or planned systems already address similar requirements (past projects or current pipelines). If yes, additional licenses or reuse may suffice instead of a new silo.

Think at group/company-wide scope: look for mechanisms usable across the whole organization, not only inside one’s own IT unit; coordinate with related companies and overseas IT organizations to optimize IT solutions.

Do not take user requirements at face value. User departments are often unclear about what they truly need from a system; the internal SE, as an IT professional, must understand the real desired outcomes and problems to be solved, then propose accordingly.

First-year internal SEs have limited knowledge and experience; do not try to design mechanisms alone. Use supervisors and project managers, and build business-contributing systems as a team rather than solving everything solo.

Siloing is avoided by combining future-oriented strategy checks, reuse of existing systems, group-wide thinking, deep inquiry into real user needs, and team consultation rather than isolated local solutions.
In-house SE (社内SE) contributes to projects from the IT side; they need not take on everything dumped by proposers, including work the proposer themselves should consider.
If in-house SE absorbs that work, the proposing department is only avoiding its own issues via manpower rather than solving them at the root.
Staff shortages may stem from how the organization allocates priorities, or from weak hiring power (company appeal and branding).
To keep the organization functioning, clearly separate what in-house SE should do from what the proposer should do, and proceed with the proposal (起案) phase on that basis.

A former boss of the author would reject unprepared business units in the proposal phase with “If you haven’t even considered it, this is a waste of time—come back after you’ve thought it through.” Most people cannot take that hard line, so a milder approach is needed.
The proposal phase involves a limited number of people, so do not rigidly apply full project-management methods or heavy deliverable definitions.
Without any defined deliverables or milestones, meetings alone waste time.

The key is for in-house SE to lay some rails for the business department: understand what must be done in the proposal phase, explain the process, schedule the tasks, and prompt the necessary considerations.
In-house SEs who can support proposers’ thinking in this way will be increasingly needed as IT demand spreads across more domains and they become the hub of those IT considerations.
Purpose of role division in the proposal phase is to be understood via five steps (役割分担の目的 / 5つのステップ / 起案フェーズの役割分担を理解する).
Internal SEs (社内SE) must proactively lay the rails (set structure and process) for project initiation with business departments, because those departments often lack project experience.
Step 1: Use self-introduction to understand the counterpart. Business-department staff may be project amateurs even after 5–10 years in the department; assess how much support they will need.

Step 2: Confirm internal processes and deadlines before planning begins (e.g., next-fiscal-year project-application cutoff). This determines the required speed of consideration; verify with a superior.

Step 3: Assess the current state of consideration in the business department (it may already be advanced or still rudimentary). Identify the proposer and the necessary next actions. In the first meeting, check status against the inputs required for the proposal document (shown in Figure 5-3).

Step 4: Accelerate consideration by requesting a ‘tatakidai’ (rough draft / straw-man). Set a sharing deadline. A draft has a much lower creation hurdle than a formal deliverable. The proposal phase involves repeated trial-and-error, so treat outputs as drafts to keep momentum.

If a proposer fails to produce even the agreed draft by the deadline, stop. Forcing the initiation phase through will likely produce the same failure in later phases. Execution ability is required to run a project; halt before the project officially starts.
Step 5: Once draft-making is agreed, schedule regular meetings (定例会). Regular meetings reduce one-off scheduling overhead and give the proposer a cadence to progress against.

In business-department-initiated projects involving internal SEs, the proposing department must always drive certain areas of the work; the IT department should not be expected to execute the entire project on its own even if the share of IT-related consideration varies.
A project’s measures consist of an IT domain that is only a subset of the whole plus non-IT measures; progress requires advancing both, not treating IT as the entirety of the project.
The subject (owner) of the project remains the proposing department; when that department is a business unit, IT and non-IT actions are mixed and both must be pursued.
A common misconception (illustrated as the right-hand side of Figure 5-8) is that the IT domain fills 100 % of the project’s measures, leading people to dump all work onto the IT department.
The underlying cause of the misconception is low IT literacy among internal staff; internal SEs should therefore help raise that literacy rather than simply absorb the dumped work.
Figure 5-8 contrasts the correct project structure (IT as only part of the measures) with the mistaken structure (IT occupying the entire project).
Japanese companies often struggle to keep up with the rapid pace of IT evolution because many lack personnel who can provide IT education.

Japan's lifetime employment system (終身雇用制度) still results in relatively low talent mobility compared with overseas, even though job-type employment (ジョブ型雇用) has increased. Consequently, business- or operations-department staff who have already run multiple projects are rarely recruited into similar projects at other companies.
High-IT-literacy talent inside a company is limited, so education that raises IT literacy is important.
Once the direction of a system introduction becomes clear, the internal SE (社内SE) should help raise IT literacy. Two practical methods are recommended.

Method 1 – Learn at solution seminars: When the introduction direction is visible, encourage attendance at seminars run by leading solutions in that domain. For packages or SaaS, the implementing SIer or package vendor typically holds regular seminars. Both the internal SE and the proposing department's staff should attend together.

Method 2 – Learn from companies that have already implemented: Many firms have already solved similar problems. If they are in a different industry they are not competitors and often willingly give lectures. If no personal connections exist, acquaintances made with package vendors at the seminars in Method 1 can provide introductions.
A first-year internal SE is almost never expected to steer these two methods, but as one advances to project-manager or higher roles such initiatives become necessary.
When assigned to a system-introduction project in an unfamiliar domain, it is highly effective for an internal SE to apply independently to relevant seminars early in order to raise domain knowledge.
超概算見積もり (ultra-rough estimate) is the process of calculating a broad, high-level budget required for a project.
First-year in-house SEs are almost never asked to produce ultra-rough estimates, but preparing for them from the first year is still valuable.
Ultra-rough estimates are based on personal experience used to secure a budget; first-year in-house SEs lack that experience, so estimation viewpoints are provided instead.

Development-cost viewpoints for ultra-rough estimates include: system license fees (package or SaaS usage fees); system construction fees paid to an SIer; interface-design costs for linking with existing systems; tester costs for outsourcing system tests (e.g., to SES); and various infrastructure-construction costs needed to build the system.
Operation-cost viewpoints for ultra-rough estimates include: various infrastructure costs (cloud usage fees, server maintenance, etc.) and post-release operation/maintenance costs.
Figure 5-9 organizes these viewpoints into 開発コスト (development costs) and 運用コスト (operation costs) as a practical framework for producing an ultra-rough project budget.
When using SaaS, construction costs may be kept low, but running (operational) costs can exceed those savings and must be considered in the estimate.
For large-scale projects, a certain amount of travel and transportation expenses should be included in the cost estimate.
A buffer (contingency/reserve fund, 予備費) for unexpected situations should be added to the estimate; the amount is decided in consultation with the project owner.
System modification projects are relatively easy to estimate because quotes can be obtained by inquiring with the existing vendor.
Introducing a new mechanism or system is much harder to estimate than modifying an existing one.
Combining multiple sources of estimate information (the options below) can raise the accuracy of the overall estimate.

Estimate-information options (図5-10): ① Web price search — package or SaaS prices can sometimes be confirmed on the web; ② Consult third-party organizations — use reporting-service companies or consulting firms; ③ Interview internal experts — if the company already has an implementation, ask the person in charge; ④ Estimate from own experience — rough calculation based on personal experience (high hurdle for a first-year internal SE, becomes possible with accumulated experience); ⑤ Direct inquiry to vendors — sales activity starts from the moment of inquiry, so timing must be adjusted.
Caveat on option ④: without relevant experience the figure is merely a guess, not a reliable estimate.
Caveat on option ⑤: communicating with vendors risks triggering unnecessary sales activity; inquiry timing must therefore be carefully coordinated.
Internal approval processes (社内承認プロセス) must be carefully sequenced and planned; otherwise they consume unexpected time and drag down the project.
The most important starting point is how the approval process is perceived: treating it as a wasteful formality prevents it from being used productively.

Some approval steps may have become hollow or ritualized, but their essential function is a company checkpoint (関所) that communicates the concept to the right people, secures budget, and obtains a GO sign to proceed.
A first-year in-house SE attending an approval judgment meeting (承認判定会議) should prepare all necessary information openly and approach the meeting wanting problems to be pointed out.

Approval meetings should be viewed positively as a project health-check; obtaining the approver’s endorsement (お墨付き) lets the project proceed with confidence, so the meeting should be treated as borrowing the approver’s support (胸を借りる).
Actual approval processes differ by company; required content and precision also differ by project phase, so the expected level of detail at each gate must be understood in advance.

In the proposal/initiation phase (起案フェーズ) measures and budget figures are still rough and high-level; this is expected, and failing to recognize it leads to spending excessive time on premature concretization.

In the proposal (起案) phase, proposed measures are deliberated from IT strategy and cost-effectiveness viewpoints to decide whether consideration should be promoted. Approving measures that diverge from strategy or lack expected effects prevents effective allocation of people, goods, and money (ヒト・モノ・カネ) in the organization. At this stage, both measure content and budget are typically rough estimates.

In the launch (立ち上げ) phase, measure content is fleshed out, cost-effectiveness is scrutinized, and whether the project should actually be started is deliberated. Confirmation that preparations such as organizational structure (体制) are in place is also performed.
In the construction (構築) phase, unexpected changes arise as the project proceeds. This phase deliberates whether to approve those changes (e.g., budget or development-scope changes).

Nemawashi (根回し) is prior information sharing needed to advance the approval process. Sharing information with the right people before the approval-judgment meeting to raise review accuracy is acceptable. Having approvers identify issues in advance, correcting them, and then attending the meeting is also acceptable. Because the approval process exists as a checkpoint (関所) to make the project meaningful, activities that raise project quality should be recommended.

Approval content by phase (各フェーズにおける承認内容): Proposal (起案) — judge promotion of measures from strategy consistency and cost-effectiveness; timing: annual; measure precision: concept/rough; budget precision: estimate/rough. Launch (立ち上げ) — judge whether to start the project after making measures concrete; timing: at project start; measure precision: outline/high; budget precision: estimate/high. Construction (構築) — approve changes to budget or development scope; timing: as needed (随時); measure precision: specific; budget precision: N/A.
Decide who, when, and to what granularity business process flows (業務フロー) will be prepared; then the internal SE supports the business department in creating those flows.
Before project start, raise internal IT literacy via training on the planned system and hearings with companies that have already implemented it.
The approval process is a checkpoint (関所): convey the concept to the right people in the company, secure budget, obtain the GO sign, and then proceed with the project.
Beware of skipping the project's original purpose that should be examined, so that systemization (the means) does not become the purpose itself.
IT solution consideration must not only meet users' functional requirements; it must comprehensively factor in IT strategy, the existing system landscape, and similar constraints.
Requirements tend to silo. Check whether the same requirement is already being handled by another department, and whether the case can be integrated with other departments' work.
For an internal SE, the real failure is when a case is never even made into a project and is never considered at all.

The 立ち上げフェーズ (project launch/initiation phase) is a critical process after requirements definition that determines the actual direction of system construction; preparation in this phase can make or break the subsequent construction phase.

In the launch phase, the project's system-construction direction is set, including rules, governance, organizational structure (体制), the system itself, SIer involvement, and role assignments, before actual system building begins.
Figure 6-1 (立ち上げフェーズの重要性) illustrates that the launch phase decides the direction of system construction and feeds that direction, along with rules and governance, into later phases.
Chapter 6 is framed around three core questions: What is needed to launch a project? How should RFI/RFP be carried out? What is a PoC (Proof of Concept)?

Project launch (立ち上げ) preparation differs by situation: in-house or enhancement development does not require SIer selection; estimates and organization building proceed with the in-house development team or existing operations/maintenance vendor.
When introducing a new package, SIer selection is required using RFI/RFP based on requirements from the project proposal, followed by negotiation with the SIer.
Internal organization building for full-scale project operation should proceed in parallel with vendor selection and negotiation.
Even first-year in-house SEs (社内SE 1年生) are likely to be assigned actual tasks in the launch phase and therefore need to understand each task.
Launch-phase process when system/SIer is not already selected: RFI/RFP → PoC → contract/price negotiation → internal/external organization building → project start.

Chapter 6 topics covering the launch phase include: 立ち上げフェーズ, RFI/RFP, ベンダーリスト (vendor list), 役割分担表 (role assignment table), 提案プロセス (proposal process), デモとプレゼン (demo and presentation), 提案内容の評価 (proposal evaluation), PoC, 契約の準備 (contract preparation), 価格交渉の準備 (price negotiation preparation), 体制構築 (organization building), and 人の巻き込み (getting people involved).
The initiation/startup phase (立ち上げフェーズ) of a project produces a set of related contractual and procurement documents; these terms are both vocabulary for the phase and its deliverables.
NDA / Non-Disclosure Agreement (秘密保持契約書): a document in which parties promise not to leak the company’s confidential information; it is required in order to start the engagement.
RFI / Request For Information (情報提供依頼書): a document sent to prospective vendors asking them to provide information such as products they handle, services, and past track records.
RFP / Request For Proposal (提案依頼書): a document sent to prospective vendors asking them to propose system-development services or products.

MSA / Master Service Agreement (基本契約書): a master contract exchanged with a product vendor or SIer. When an MSA exists, individual contracts and SOWs are created based on it (e.g., SIer man-month rates).
Individual contract (個別契約書): a project-specific contract created on the basis of the MSA. Because the MSA is general, the individual contract addresses matters unique to that project.
SOW / Statement of Work (作業範囲記述書): a document that defines the scope of work and serves as the premise for estimates when an individual contract is executed.

In the overall flow (Figure 6-4), the conception/proposal phase (起案フェーズ) sits above the startup phase; the startup phase takes the content examined in the conception phase as its input for systems and related terms.

The project launch phase (立ち上げフェーズ) takes as input the outputs of the drafting/proposal phase (起案フェーズ), including target service, To-Be and As-Is business flows, existing services, issues and their solutions, business initiatives, development overview, cost-effectiveness, and project duration.

Key launch-phase processes are: building the organization needed to start the project (体制構築), signing NDAs (秘密保持契約), creating RFI/RFP and requesting vendor proposals, evaluating vendor proposals, contract and price negotiation, obtaining formal internal approval, signing contracts with vendors, and building the development organization.
Typical deliverables include organization charts (体制図), NDA, RFI, RFP, evaluation sheets (評価表), estimates (見積書), MSA, SOW, and approval documents (承認資料).
SIer (System Integrator) selection occurs in the launch phase. When an RFP is issued for package selection, a high-level To-Be business flow should be included so vendors can propose against it.
If To-Be business-flow work in the prior phase was insufficient, the information must be refined to an appropriate level of granularity before the RFP.
RFI/RFP（情報提供依頼書／提案依頼書）は、ベンダーに何かを提案してもらう際に使用する文書である。
RFI/RFPは起案フェーズで特定された課題を解決する手段を選ぶために使用する。
RFIは製品情報などの情報収集に利用する。
RFPは入札にあたっての提案をもらう際に活用する。
システム構築プロジェクトでは、まずどの領域をRFI/RFPの対象にするかを検討する。
既存システムのエンハンス開発の場合、ほとんどの場合は既存の運用保守に関連する領域が対象となりやすい。
RFI/RFPのプロセス: どの領域でRFI/RFPが必要か特定する → RFIで情報収集する → RFP対象企業を絞る（ベンダーリスト作成） → RFPを行う → 提案を評価しベンダーを選定する。
RFIはベンダーリストに基づく情報収集、RFPは提案書の評価とベンダー選定に用いられる。
When requesting vendor estimates for a new system implementation, you must decide which domains to include in the RFI/RFP (proposal request).
RFI/RFP consideration areas are 業務領域 (business domain), IT領域 (IT domain), and 共通領域 (common domains) such as project management.
First-year in-house SEs (社内SE 1年生) are rarely directly involved in these scoping decisions, but they need to understand the underlying thinking in order to support RFI/RFP work.
A project requires coordinated activities in the business domain, IT domain, and common domain.
Business departments often assume that once the system license and the implementing SIer are chosen, the project can proceed; more scoping of work is actually required.
Three typical RFP-scope patterns exist: (1) request all domains from the vendor, (2) request only the IT domain from the vendor, (3) request only development from the vendor.

In the accompanying figure (図6-6 RFP実施領域の選択肢), green text marks work requested from the vendor and black text marks work performed in-house; items shown include 業務標準化 (business standardization), システムライセンス (system license), システム導入 (system implementation), and 全体プロジェクトマネジメント (overall project management).

When planning who will execute a project, it is a common misconception that only the IT domain proceeds; in reality, it is also necessary to decide who will carry out the business-domain work and the project-management domain.

Example activity split (Figure 6-6): the business domain may include business-standardization activities, the IT domain may include license purchase and implementation activities, and overall project-management activities exist as a common layer across both.

Pattern ① — Request all domains from the vendor: both the business domain and the IT domain are proposed by the vendor. This approach is used when internal resources are exhausted or when the company has no specialized internal department. Advantage: the project can more easily be advanced in lockstep with business transformation.

Pattern ② — Request only the IT domain from the vendor: the vendor leads from system proposal through implementation and proposes a system that satisfies the issues and requirements written in the RFP. Accompanying business-transformation work is assumed to be performed with internal resources.

Pattern ③ — Request only development/implementation from the vendor: used when the system has already been selected; the vendor is asked only for a proposal covering the system-implementation portion.

RFI (Request for Information / 情報提供依頼書) is used to request information about products or services that are not publicly available on the Web, etc. RFP (Request for Proposal) is used to request proposals concerning candidate products or services.

RFI/RFP document items should be tailored to the project. Example item — Background and purpose: describe why the company needs the current project and what the initiative is intended to achieve. In an RFI this section is kept concise; in an RFP it is made more concrete. This item appears in both RFI and RFP.

RFI/RFP documents for vendor selection in IT project kickoff should include a company introduction (自社紹介), because vendors have industry- and business-type-specific strengths and weaknesses; provide an overview of the company's business.
Specify desired proposal content (提案内容): whether general product proposals are wanted or proposals from an SIer for system implementation.
Include a timeline (タイムライン) covering RFI/RFP response deadlines and, for RFPs, subsequent demo and presentation schedule.
Provide contact information (連絡先) as the inquiry window for the RFI/RFP.
State prerequisites and bidding requirements (前提条件・応札要件) that vendors must understand or that bidders must satisfy.
Describe the project schedule (プロジェクトスケジュール), including the target date for achieving project goals and any desired milestones.
Define project scope (プロジェクトスコープ): company-wide vs. limited domain, and whether only SIer system-construction support is required or also business support.
Outline expected organization and role sharing (体制・役割分担). Sharing a RASCI chart clarifies vendor expectations; role-sharing misunderstandings affect estimates and are therefore important.
Provide supplementary materials (補足資料) such as As-Is/To-Be business flows, IT roadmap, and existing system landscape from the proposal phase, to the extent they can be disclosed.
For package implementations, include a functional-requirements list (機能要求一覧) so vendors can indicate whether their product can implement or support each function.
If product demos or proposal presentations are planned, include a demo/presentation overview (デモ・プレゼン概要). If details are not yet fixed at RFP time, state that they will be communicated later.

A vendor list enumerates the vendors (typically SIers) that will be invited to submit proposals via RFI/RFP; it must be deliberately assembled because the market contains many vendors and failing to list them risks receiving proposals only from long-standing familiar partners rather than those best able to meet the company’s actual requirements.
Some organizations assign the indirect-purchasing department to support vendor-list creation; the in-house SE should therefore confirm the company’s own process rather than assume a uniform approach.
A first-year in-house SE is not expected to decide unilaterally which vendors receive an RFI/RFP, but is often given a supporting role in information gathering and list preparation.

Internal expert interviews are a primary information source: superiors, the CIO and other IT-department specialists, plus overseas subsidiaries, other business units and affiliated companies, expand the search and also surface questions that will later appear in the project-start approval process (for example, “Why did we choose solution B when a similar subsidiary chose A?” or “Why was integration onto A never considered?”).

Third-party analyst firms such as Gartner publish comparative evaluations and reports of solutions; these reports are relatively easy to obtain through ordinary internet search and can be used to populate or validate a vendor list.

When launching a project and selecting package software, attend vendor seminars: package vendors often hold them regularly. You will mainly hear the vendor's strengths, but seminars can rapidly raise product knowledge.

Collect first-hand feedback from companies that have already implemented the package. Vendors may introduce reference customers via seminars, or invite those companies to share real experiences. Use those connections to interview them, but note the bias: you typically hear from firms that are at least somewhat satisfied with the product.

Internet search is useful for vendor research, with two cautions: (1) market leaders tend to rank at the top of results; (2) vendor-created competitor comparisons are subjective to that vendor. Always consider who published the information and from what standpoint.

Figure 6-8 frames information collection as a funnel: gather widely from experts (有識者), third-party organizations (第三者機関), vendor lists (ベンダーリスト), seminars (セミナー), implemented companies (導入済み企業), and web search (ネット検索), then extract a shortlist of target vendors.

A common project failure is role-division misunderstandings with an SIer (system integrator), which cause cost overruns and schedule delays. Prevent this by using a role-assignment table that makes clear who performs which role.

The role-assignment table is also called RASCI: R (Responsible) = person who executes the work; A (Accountable) = person who is ultimately answerable; S (Support) = supporter; C (Consulted) = person to consult; I (Informed) = person to be reported to or kept informed. A variant without S is RACI.
Walk through the RASCI matrix with internal stakeholders to reach consensus on expected work. Attach the same RASCI to the RFP so expected roles can be aligned with the vendor.
Example RASCI layout (Figure 6-9): left columns list phase, item and work content; right columns assign R/A/S/C/I to 業務部門 (business department), 社内SE (in-house SE) and SIer.

Requirements-definition phase mappings: 要求定義 (define business requirements) — 業務部門 R/A, 社内SE S/I, SIer C; 機能定義 (convert business requirements into functional specs) — 業務部門 A/S, 社内SE S/I, SIer R; システム仕様定義 (define system specs from functional definition) — 業務部門 I, 社内SE A/S, SIer R.

Architecture mappings: ソリューションアーキテクチャ定義 (design overall system architecture) — 業務部門 I, 社内SE A/S, SIer R; エンタープライズアーキテクチャ定義 (design enterprise-wide architecture in the system landscape) — 業務部門 I, 社内SE R, SIer A/S.
RASCI is used both to attach to an RFP so vendors can submit proposals and estimates, and to build internal consensus on roles among stakeholders.

When it is still unclear whether the company will perform a given task itself, temporarily assign R (Responsible) to the vendor so the work is included in the proposal and does not become a later budget problem.
RASCI should be reviewed with key internal people before the RFP is issued; otherwise later-phase members who first encounter the matrix risk role misunderstandings.

Internal RASCI confirmation should cover these categories: project management (whether the vendor owns overall PM or only the development portion); requirements definition (how far the vendor supports work such as As-Is/To-Be process design, aligned with business units); data integration (in-house vs. vendor effort for migrating data from existing systems); testing (degree of vendor involvement in test preparation and support); training (which user populations the vendor trains—all staff vs. a limited group); rollout/implementation (which sites the vendor supports when there are multiple locations); and post-release support (how long the vendor remains on standby after go-live).
Once the RFP and RASCI are ready, proposals are requested from vendors.
Figure 6-11 is a more detailed breakdown of the proposal-request and proposal-evaluation process shown in Figure 6-4 (page 123).
For evaluation, evaluation axes (criteria) are created and arrangements are made for vendor demos and presentations.

NDA (non-disclosure agreement) must be confirmed before sending the RFP: RFI does not disclose highly confidential company information, but RFP does because it is needed for vendors to prepare proposals.
RFP send timing should be aligned across vendors so the process remains fair.
Proposal-request flow: send RFP → conduct Q&A as needed → receive vendor responses.
Proposal-evaluation flow: evaluate RFP content → hold demos/presentations → perform final evaluation.

When issuing RFPs to multiple vendors, send them at the same time so every vendor has equal preparation time; a delayed send to even one of (for example) 10 vendors can leave that vendor with insufficient time and create unfair differences in proposal quality. Fairness is a core requirement of the RFP process.

Attach a Q&A fill-in list to the RFP so vendors can submit questions. Answers must be distributed to all vendors, including those who did not ask questions, to prevent information gaps between bidders.

Even if a junior in-house SE is not chosen as an official evaluator (which is typical for first-year staff), they should still score proposals independently. Comparing one’s own criteria with the official evaluators’ viewpoints is a growth opportunity.

The vendor-facing RFP timeline should (1) give vendors enough time and (2) make explicit when the client will provide information and when vendors must submit materials. The final selection date can be left vague (e.g., “around the end of July”) as insurance: large projects with many stakeholders often delay final decisions, and a fuzzy date helps deflect vendor follow-up after RFP work is finished.

Example vendor-published timeline: 6/1 RFP sent; 6/2–6/12 email and face-to-face Q&A; 6/20 RFP response deadline; 6/21–6/25 proposal evaluation and tailored demos; 7/1 primary selection results and custom-demo briefing; 7/2–7/10 custom demos; end of July final selection results.

After receiving vendor proposals in response to an RFP, organizations should not only review the written proposals but also have vendors conduct product demos and presentations to obtain additional information.

Internal SEs should treat vendor demos and presentations not merely as selection opportunities but as learning opportunities for themselves and company members to be exposed to external IT technologies and implementation know-how.

Tailor-made demo (for systems/services): Performed to understand a product's general usage methods and standard functions. Used for primary screening when there are many candidate systems or services. Because it is a generic demo, it is difficult to judge whether it satisfies specific RFP requirements.

Custom demo (for systems/services): Unlike a tailor-made demo, it reflects the company's own use cases and RFP request contents. Enables verification of how the company's requirements can be met. Data collaboration with the vendor may be required for the demo. Typically used in final selection stages.
Presentation (for implementation SIer): Explanation by the vendor of their proposal contents in response to the RFP, such as the system construction approach.

System selection and vendor (SIer) selection may be conducted separately; however, depending on RFP requirements, vendors may be asked to propose both the system/service and its implementation together.

Demos and presentations in the RFP process serve the purpose of gathering further information beyond written proposals and should be requested from vendors accordingly (as illustrated in Figure 6-13).

In vendor selection via RFP, skipping tailor-made demos and starting directly with custom demos may appear more efficient for judging whether a system meets in-house requirements, but this approach has important caveats.

RFP demos and presentations are valuable learning opportunities. Custom demos are based only on the company's stated requirements, creating a risk of missing functions that would be beneficial but are not currently requested.

Example: A company seeking to streamline order receiving and shipping can compare that area in a custom demo, yet would not discover AI-powered automatic order sorting or automatic warehouse expansion features that are absent from current requirements but could yield large future efficiency gains.
Recommended sequence: first use tailor-made demos to broaden general knowledge of typical capabilities, then confirm how those capabilities can address the company's specific requirements.

Custom demos require substantial effort. Preparing them with every candidate vendor consumes considerable man-hours. A practical approach is to run tailor-made demos first, narrow the field to a few vendors, conduct Q&A so those vendors understand the requirements, and only then hold custom demos.

Narrowing the vendor list raises the quality of information provided to vendors and the quality of their proposals, which in turn increases the likelihood of selecting a system that actually matches the company's needs.
These considerations constitute key caution points when planning product demos during project launch and vendor evaluation.
There is no unique correct answer when evaluating options for selection; the optimal product or service depends on what the project prioritizes.
Evaluations consist of quantitative evaluation and qualitative evaluation; project stakeholders must form consensus and decide the weights of the evaluation criteria.
For proceeding with evaluation, internal roles must be defined. In large projects, some stakeholders should not evaluate due to responsibility or capability reasons.

Three evaluation roles: Decision maker (意思決定者) — the person who makes the final decision based on the evaluators’ scores; Evaluator (評価者) — the person who scores based on proposal content and demo content; Contributor (コントリビューター) — a person who may participate in demos and give opinions but does not directly evaluate.

Evaluation framework (Who / What / How): Who = who evaluates and who makes the final decision; What = evaluation axes (viewpoints) and how their weights are set; How = tools and documents used for the evaluation work (and preparation for evaluation).

Example evaluation axes (What): company capability evaluation (企業力評価), implementation track record evaluation (導入実績評価), organizational structure/system evaluation (体制評価), function evaluation (機能評価), demo evaluation (デモ評価), and price evaluation (価格評価).

In project launch (プロジェクト立ち上げ), the evaluator assessment process is supported by defining evaluation axes (評価軸). Evaluators score according to those axes; aggregated results are then used by decision-makers such as the project owner for approval (決裁).

Example evaluation axes (評価軸) and their contents: 企業力 (corporate strength) = 企業の信頼性 (company reliability); 導入実績 (implementation track record) = similar industry or business-type deployments; 体制 (team/organization) = structure of members assigned to the project; 機能 (functionality) = degree of fulfillment of functional requirements (機能要求の充足度); テーラーメイド・カスタムデモ (tailor-made/custom demo) = product demonstration; 価格 (price) = price and contract terms.
Typical vendor-selection flow: perform a primary screening of all candidates, then invite only the remaining two companies to deliver custom demos, and use those demos for the final evaluation.

Weighted scoring example (評価結果): 企業力 10 %, 導入実績 15 %, 体制 15 %, 機能 20 %, テーラーメイドデモ 20 %, 価格 20 %. After primary scoring, only companies A and B proceed to custom demos; the combined results lead to a recommendation of company B’s product to the decision-maker.
In the illustrated scoring table all six vendors quoted the same price (1 億円); custom-demo scores were then applied only to the two shortlisted vendors (A: 15, B: 20).
The purpose of a project is to contribute to the business; advancing or promoting the project itself is not the purpose.

It is important to do one's best to proceed according to predetermined milestones, but even more important is to properly escalate and take appropriate action when necessary preparations are not in place.
PoC (Proof of Concept / 机上検証・概念実証) is used to verify unclear parts of a project, clarifying opaque areas and reducing the risk of failure.

Example of PoC use: When introducing a solution, after receiving explanations and demos, if it remains unclear whether the solution meets the company's requirements, conduct partial desk verification via PoC.
The purpose of PoC is to determine a clear yes/no (black and white) through verification. Conducting PoC vaguely without first clarifying the viewpoints to be verified constitutes a failed PoC.
PoC process steps: (1) Identify the part to be verified, (2) Define the verification goal, (3) Prepare for verification, (4) Conduct the verification, (5) Make a judgment.
Step (1) must first be agreed upon within the project.
If step (2) defining the goal is neglected, a PoC may be completed yet the team still proceeds into the production project with lingering uncertainty.
Preparation (step 3) depends on what is being verified; for example, obtain necessary proposals from the vendor. Development may incur costs, but depending on negotiation the vendor may cover them.
After verification, compare results against the originally defined goals and then make a judgment.
Conduct PoC as needed.

PoC (Proof of Concept) requires clearly defining and narrowing down the specific viewpoints/aspects to verify, then sharing them with all stakeholders. If these verification points are not well understood within the project, even vendor-driven PoC work can become ineffective because people start worrying about issues that do not actually need verification.
Do not let PoC drag on. Spending too much time on PoC can sap the momentum of the subsequent production project. Consciously apply appropriate scoping, rapid verification, and quick decision-making.

Clarify in advance who will make the go/no-go judgment. The purpose of PoC is to decide whether to proceed with the production project. Uncertainty is inherent in decisions, so even completing the planned verifications will not eliminate all anxieties. The person who holds final responsibility for the judgment must be designated beforehand.

Plan in advance how PoC outputs will merge into the production project. Partially verified information and system environments built for PoC can, if planned well, be reused directly in production development. Although PoC results may lead to stopping consideration of a system, also planning the success scenario in advance raises the chance of advancing the overall project efficiently.

Consider a dedicated budget for PoC. Although PoC is sometimes performed as part of a vendor’s sales activity (even for free), unsatisfactory verification is meaningless. The orthodox approach is to clarify the points that must be confirmed, discuss them with the vendor, and proceed under a contract. Contracting allows deliverables to be defined, which raises the quality of the PoC.

The most important rule in vendor contracts is never to start (or allow) development without a signed contract (NO先行着手 / no prior commencement). Informal conversations about existing-system modifications can slide into unpaid or disputed work if a vendor has spare engineering capacity.
Work performed without a contract always leads to trouble because payment is still owed once work is done; therefore contract-less commencement is forbidden.

Standard contracting sequence when nothing is yet signed: (1) company-to-company NDA, (2) RFI/RFP and vendor selection, (3) price/contract negotiation, (4) project-specific contract, then project start. Skipping the NDA creates a risk that confidential information leaks to other parties.

Two contracting patterns exist: sign a Master Service Agreement (MSA / 基本契約書) first and then individual project contracts under it, or conclude individual contracts without an MSA. The project team must decide which pattern to use.
When preparing individual contracts, the two main Japanese legal forms to understand are 請負契約 (contract of work / results-based) and 準委任契約 (quasi-mandate / effort-based service contract).
Illustrated flow (Figure 6-17): NDA締結 → RFI/RFP提案実施 → システム／ベンダー選定・確定 → 契約・価格交渉 → 契約締結, involving both the client (自社) and the vendor.

In Japanese IT project contracting (especially for in-house SE / 社内SE work with vendors), the two common types are 請負契約 (ukeoi keiyaku: lump-sum / contract for work) and 準委任契約 (jun-inin keiyaku: quasi-mandate / time-and-materials style).

請負契約: The contracted estimated amount is paid; the vendor bears responsibility for completing the deliverables (成果物の完成責任). Risk: missed items in the original estimate require additional cost. Commonly used with waterfall development. Examples: small-scale modification projects; the construction/build phase of waterfall projects.

準委任契約: Payment is based on actual development effort/man-hours; the vendor bears responsibility for performing the work (業務遂行責任) rather than guaranteeing a finished product. Unexpected work can often be adjusted if it stays within contracted hours. Risks: cost impact from assigned staff skill shortfalls causing overtime, or delays caused by the vendor’s other projects. Examples: small-to-large modification projects; waterfall requirements definition or post-release support; agile development.
Both contract types have trade-offs (一長一短). An in-house SE supporting contracting must communicate closely with the project manager and proceed carefully because the choice is highly consequential.

Never neglect the contract: do not blindly trust the vendor and skip reading it. For foreign (外資系) vendors especially, the contract is everything. When problems occur, the contract and SOW (Statement of Work / 作業範囲記述書) are the only reliable basis. In long projects the original staff may have left, leaving only the written contract.
Always personally read the contract. Check payment terms: when and how much is paid, because this interacts with the company’s budgeting process.

Always address change management and trouble handling in the contract. Unexpected events will occur; the parties must agree in advance on the process/schema for changing contract scope and document it in the contract.

When choosing between projects with different cost estimates (e.g., a 1 million yen project versus a 10 million yen project), select the one with the higher return on investment (ROI) within budget rather than the cheaper option; judgment must focus on delivered value, not the size of the amount.

Example of ROI-based project selection: a 1 million yen project that produces 200,000 yen of annual benefit versus a 10 million yen project that produces 10 million yen of annual benefit—the latter should be chosen because of its superior value.
ROI is only one decision axis; other factors such as statutory or legal requirements can also determine whether a project proceeds.
Vendor estimates must be scrutinized by reading them thoroughly; never skip reading because the vendor is familiar or the document is long, as unread proposals leave no room for negotiation.

The term 'custom correspondence' (or custom support) in vendor proposals has no standard definition and may actually mean additional development; confirm the associated costs, maintainability, and whether software updates for non-standard functionality apply automatically or require extra work.
Core principle: evaluate the price paid against the value received; prepare confirmation points on estimates in order to negotiate price effectively.

When comparing vendor estimates (e.g., Company A at 100 million yen vs. Company B at 80 million yen), compare on an apples-to-apples basis. If one estimate omits work such as organizing business requirements, it is impossible to know which is truly cheaper. Estimates cannot be compared when conditions and premises differ.

Validate engineer cost reasonableness: check for gaps between proposed engineer level and unit price (e.g., an SE billed at a manager rate). Confirm rates match inter-company agreed amounts (or historical rates if none exist) and that the right roles are assigned to each phase (consultants are not needed during development; large numbers of developers are not needed after release).

Read all footnotes, notes, and assumptions at the bottom of an estimate; they must not be skipped. Critical items such as “data loading into the product is assumed to be performed by the client” are often buried there and, if missed, become sources of vendor–client misunderstanding.

Examine license contracts carefully. System and SaaS licenses use varied billing models (CPU licenses, user counts, etc.). Understand the model and confirm purchase timing, because licenses may be unnecessary in early requirements definition or user counts may be limited at the first release site.

When internal project experience is limited and uncertainties remain after review, ask the vendor directly what is not included in the estimate. This both surfaces unknowns and tests the vendor’s sincerity as a partner.
Even an excellent proposal is worthless (a pie in the sky) unless the project can actually be completed; people and organizational structure (体制) are a critical success factor.
Build project organization using a defined process (Figure 6-19) so that the right people are assigned.
Create an organization chart (体制図) as a communication tool that makes stakeholder responsibilities and roles explicit and visualizes the cooperative structure.
The organization chart must be prepared jointly by the business department (業務部門) and the IT department; it is never solely an IT-department task.
A first-year in-house SE (社内SE 1年生) should not start an organization-chart draft from a blank PowerPoint slide; reuse existing templates or options because a blank start is too high a hurdle.

Organization-building process toward requirements definition (要件定義): create a draft, review the draft with stakeholders (an activity where a first-year SE can contribute), involve people, select personnel, and formally assign them to the project.
Personnel selection is usually based on experience rather than a talent database, so a first-year in-house SE typically finds it difficult to contribute at the selection step.
When creating a draft (たたき台) of a project organization/structure, two main options are: referring to past internal projects, and obtaining templates from vendors.

Referring to past projects is useful for learning internal writing conventions and practices that are accepted in the company. Risk: when introducing a new system, internal knowledge may fail to identify all necessary roles.

Obtaining templates from vendors is often well-received because it also serves as a sales opportunity for the vendor. It allows learning the essence of organizational structures used at other companies.
Internet search is the easiest method, but useful information about project organizational structures is almost never publicly available on the web.

After the draft is complete, have it reviewed by the project manager or responsible person to receive advice. Projects are teamwork; especially when inexperienced, leverage superiors and the PM to improve quality.

Once roles are defined in the organization chart, identify the actual people internally. If talent information is not well organized in the company, identification relies on experience/rules of thumb, so a first-year in-house SE can contribute only in a limited way.

When involving people in the project, communicate with both the assigned person and their supervisor. Tell the assignee about the project content and have them recognize their role. Obtain the supervisor’s permission to prioritize that person’s resources for this project. Without supervisor alignment, tasks from other projects may still land on the person and affect quality.
Project assignments of people must be made official in some form. The method varies by company (e.g., registering in a management ledger if a project-portfolio management department exists).

If project assignments are not made official, assigned staff may be double-booked onto other projects; creating an environment that lets people concentrate on the project is necessary. One way to formalize assignment is listing names on materials submitted to an approval or go/no-go meeting.
Project organization charts (体制図) should be designed with the understanding that required resources differ by phase, so the chart itself changes substantially across the project lifecycle.

Personnel typically increase from early phases toward the construction/build phase. Major phases to plan around are: 起案 (proposal/initiation), 立ち上げ (startup), 構築 (construction/build), and リリース・運用 (release and operations).

Typical role presence by phase (from the phase-resource image): Project Owner across phases; Business PL, IT PL, Project Manager, Project Leader, and PMO as the project ramps up; Business team and Development team during construction; Business operations and IT operations at release/operations.
Lines connecting people on an organization chart are reporting lines (レポートライン). Draw them by deciding who should appropriately report to whom so that proper reporting can occur.

Projects are assembled independently of the regular company organization to solve a specific issue within a defined period. Members are assigned project-specific roles that differ from their usual organizational roles.

Do not confuse the project organization/structure chart (体制図) with the company's organizational chart (組織図). Reporting of progress follows the project structure chart, typically to the IT project leader of the assigned team.
Names used in the project structure chart must be clear and easy to understand. Ambiguous labels such as 「支援チーム」(support team) fail to convey what the team actually supports.

Typical defects in a project structure chart: two Project Owners making accountability ambiguous; a report line going to an IT department manager instead of the IT Project Leader (IT PL); unclear report lines.

An improved structure chart has a single clearly identified responsible person, organized reporting relationships, easily understood team names (e.g., 業務標準化チーム / business-standardization team, 運用チーム / operations team, 開発チーム / development team), and explicit report lines.

Figure 6-22 presents a before-and-after comparison of project organization charts illustrating these principles: the “before” version has dual Project Owners, an unclear “support team,” and a report line to IT management; the “after” version clarifies the owner, uses descriptive team names, and shows a clean report line to the IT PL.
After completing an organizational chart (体制図), you must actually involve people in the project and secure resources; merely writing names on the chart is not sufficient.
Adjust work priorities and related factors so that project participation does not cause overwork for the people involved.
People involvement in a project should be performed using both bottom-up and top-down approaches.
Bottom-up involvement is viable when the target person has discretion to choose which project to join.
A first-year internal SE (社内SE 1年生) typically has limited authority, so they must make bottom-up requests and also negotiate with the target person's supervisor or manager.
Project stakeholders include people directly in the project structure as well as people on the system-user side.
When mobilizing a group, it is important to consider which type of person to start moving first.
Groups contain three types of people: Leader (リーダー), Follower (フォロワー), and Against (アゲインスト).
Top-down involvement approach: a request from someone with authority; used when the distance to the person is far or when the person has no discretion to choose.
Bottom-up involvement approach: a request at the field/operational level; used when the distance to the person is close or when the person has discretion to choose.
In project kickoff (プロジェクト立ち上げ), the first people to involve should be identified using a group typology of リーダー (leaders), フォロワー (followers), and アゲインスト (againsts/opposition).
Leaders are cooperative, have speaking power and influence over followers, and should be identified and persuaded first; without winning them, followers cannot be brought on board.

Followers (typically 8–9 tenths of a group) take a neutral stance, do not independently show agreement or opposition, and act after leaders or againsts based on those opinions; they form the critical mass of the project and include some enthusiastic ‘semi-leaders’ who actively support.
Againsts are oppositional and critical; extensive coordination with them is often futile (‘のれんに腕押し’) and they can become obstacles, so in the worst case they should be removed from involvement.
Persuasion can sometimes convert a person into a leader.

Groups of a certain size naturally and consistently split into leaders, followers, and againsts (remaining 1–2 tenths of the population contain both leaders and againsts); knowing this regularity helps when trying to move a collective.
Strategy: prioritize identifying and persuading leaders to influence the large follower population rather than spending equal effort on all stakeholders.
RASCI (role assignment matrix/table) is effective for preventing discrepancies in role recognition among project stakeholders such as SIers.
For opaque or unclear areas, introducing a PoC (Proof of Concept) is an option; the purpose of a PoC is to determine black and white (clarify outcomes) through verification.
Resource adjustment is not merely writing names on an organization chart; it requires coordination such as changing work priorities so that assigned people do not become overworked.
Use RFI/RFP to consider means of solving issues identified in the proposal (起案) phase.
Do not treat demos and presentations solely as vendor-selection tools; use them as valuable learning opportunities to engage with external IT technologies.
A project is only a pie in the sky if it cannot be completed; the critical factor for whether a project can be completed is the organization/system = people.
The launch/startup phase is the process of building the 'project mechanism'; preparation in this phase determines the success or failure of the subsequent construction phase.

The requirements definition phase (要件定義) considers What (what means will be used to solve the problems identified in the proposal/ideation phase). The subsequent basic design phase (基本設計) then considers How (how those solution means will be implemented).
Requirements definition defines What: it specifies what is required of the system.
Defined requirements include not only system requirements (システム要件) but also business requirements (業務要件).
System requirements are only a subset of the business requirements needed to achieve the project's purpose; they are not the entirety of those business requirements.
System requirements can be properly elicited only after sufficient business consideration (業務検討) has been performed. The reverse is never possible.
A common mistake is failing to treat insufficient progress in business consideration as a problem, and instead collecting only the requirements that happen to be available and proceeding anyway.

The overall flow of Why → What → How is: Proposal/ideation phase (起案) answers Why (why a solution is needed); requirements definition answers What (what is required of the system); basic design answers How (how it will be built).
