The major purpose of requirements definition (要件定義) is not only to capture a system's functional requirements but to surface all requirements needed to achieve the project's objectives.

The requirements-definition phase must involve various stakeholders and obtain their assistance; the characteristics and interests of SIer sales (SIer営業), SIer SE, the company's business division (事業部門), and operations division (業務部門) must be understood.

Business and operations departments tend to listen to the ideals presented by SIer sales; internal SE (社内SE) tends to listen to SIer SE. This produces a mismatched requirements process in which business/ops accept the sales pitch while internal SE only explores what is technically feasible with the SIer SE.

SIer sales typically focuses on ideals; SIer SE focuses on realizability/feasibility (実現性). The resulting 'mismatched requirements definition' (噛み合わない要件定義) is a pattern that should be avoided (避けるべき要件定義).
Figure 7-3 illustrates this misalignment: business/operations departments take SIer sales proposals at face value, while internal SE jointly explores only what can be done with the SIer SE.
あるべき要件定義の構図は、関係者がプロジェクトの目的に基づいて、解決すべき課題を中心に据えることである。
社内SEは、SIer営業・SIer SE・事業部門や業務部門のフォーカスがどこに向かいやすいかを理解した上で、共通の目的と課題に視点を合わせて進められるように支援する必要がある。
社内SEがあるべきフォーカスを意識し、問題提起や問いかけをすることで関係者に気づきを促すことができる。
よほど大規模なプロジェクトでもない限り、社内SE 1年生でも貢献できる余地は十分にある。
関係者が解決すべき課題を中心に検討することで、噛み合った要件定義が可能になる。
Junior in-house SEs (社内SE 1年生) commonly become confused during requirements definition (要件定義) about which tasks they themselves should perform versus which tasks the SIer should perform.
Resolving this confusion requires understanding RASCI (covered in Chapter 6), the SIer utilization model (SIer活用モデル), development scope (開発スコープ), and deliverables (成果物).
Five SIer utilization models exist for requirements definition, illustrated in Figure 7-5.
Model ①: No SIer support (SIerの支援なし) — only the business department (業務部門) and in-house SE participate.
Model ②: IT support only (IT支援のみ) — business department, in-house SE, and SIer participate.
Model ③: Support by the same SIer (同一SIerによる支援) — business department, in-house SE, and one SIer participate.
Model ④: Support by separate SIers (別々のSIerによる支援) — business department, in-house SE, plus a SIer/business consultant and another SIer.
Model ⑤: Complete outsourcing/throwing everything to the vendor (丸投げ) — only the SIer is involved; this occurs when the preceding models fail to function.
The models typically cover the activities of business consideration (業務検討) and system requirements organization (システム要件整理).
Certain models are more common in small-to-medium projects (小～中規模プロジェクトに多い) while others appear more often in large-scale projects (大規模プロジェクトに多い).

Five models of SIer (System Integrator) involvement in requirements definition: (1) No SIer support — the company itself carries out everything from business consideration through system requirements definition; commonly used for relatively small-scale system modification projects. (2) IT support only — the company handles business consideration in-house and engages an SIer from the system-requirements-definition stage onward; seen in package introductions or medium-scale system construction when internal resources are insufficient. (3) Support by the same SIer — for large projects where in-house resources alone cannot cover both business consideration and development, one SIer supports both the business and IT domains. (4) Support by separate SIers — a business-specialist SIer supports the business side while an IT-specialist SIer supports the IT side; RASCI must be used to clarify responsibility boundaries. (5) Complete dump (丸投げ) — occurs when the business or IT department fails to fulfill its proper role: the business department starts the project but in reality dumps it onto an SIer or business consultant, and the IT department attends early meetings but never reviews deliverables.

丸投げ (complete dumping / abdication of ownership) must be absolutely avoided in requirements definition. When a project is left to the SIer, it is steered according to the SIer’s own objectives rather than the company’s.

A project consisting only of the business department and an SIer creates a “kamo-negi” (easy-mark) situation: the business department wants to buy a system and the SIer wants to sell one; such a project cannot succeed.

丸投げ is not limited to doing nothing. Even if reviews are performed, failing to steer the project back toward its original purpose and issues is equivalent to dumping. In-house SEs must act with a clear recognition of the project’s original purpose, the problems to be solved, and the role expected of them.
Key statement: “要件定義で絶対に避けなければいけないことが丸投げです。” (What must absolutely be avoided in requirements definition is dumping.) “丸投げは絶対NG” (Dumping is absolutely NG).
First-year in-house SEs must understand differences in how requirements definition proceeds and the scope the in-house SE needs to lead.
Requirements-definition approach differs by whether you build a system (scratch/custom development) or use one (package or service introduction).
When building a system: design To-Be business flow from As-Is business flow; the gap/difference becomes system demands and requirements. Fit the system to the business.
When using a system: premise is using the product’s functions and already-defined business flows, so fit the business to the system. Consider add-ons only if alignment is absolutely impossible (NG).
Core contrast: “make” vs “use” — custom work extracts gaps as requirements; packaged work jumps to fitting operations to the product except as a last resort.

In-house SEs (社内SE), especially first-years, must understand the division of responsibility (役割分担 / 守備範囲) between the SIer and the in-house SE: which scope the SIer will handle versus which parts the in-house SE must drive themselves.

Example case (Figure 7-7): business-improvement target is limited to processes B–C, with the main work being SaaS introduction into process B. Typical SIer scope then covers new-system introduction, related add-on development, the inbound interface that receives data from existing system A, and the outbound interface that sends data to existing system B.
Package or cloud-service introductions commonly use almost the same responsibility split: SIer owns the new system plus the immediately adjacent interfaces; in-house SE owns everything else.

In-house SE duties under this split: receive the new-system interface requirements, lead the detailed definition of interfaces with existing systems, and communicate with the SE teams that operate and maintain those existing systems in order to capture their requirements.

A frequent and damaging misconception is that the SIer SE will take full responsibility from existing-system interfaces all the way through new-system introduction. When each party assumes the other owns a given piece of work, requirement elicitation is skipped in those areas.

Scope-recognition misalignment (スコープの認識齟齬) maps directly onto missing requirements (要件漏れ). Successful requirements definition therefore depends on an explicit, shared picture of who owns which interfaces and which systems.

Diagram 7-7 labels processes A/B/C, existing systems A and B, the new system, and the interfaces (IF) that sit on the boundary; it visually assigns new-system introduction + add-on development + adjacent IFs to the SIer while assigning the remaining existing-system IF work and overall process ownership to the in-house SE.
In system construction (system development) projects, a set of standard terms is used across phases; these terms are important for communication with SIers (system integrators).
要求分析 (requirements analysis): organizing the wishes/desires that the system should realize.
要件定義 (requirements definition): organizing the specific requirements demanded of the system.
基本設計 (basic design): clarifying the functions to be implemented so that requirements are reflected.
詳細設計 (detailed design): breaking down the basic design to a granularity at which programmers can actually develop.
外部設計 (external design): interface design for connecting the system being developed with existing systems.
構造設計 (structural design): designing the architecture of the entire system.
機能設計 (functional design): defining each function of the system.
インターフェース設計 (interface design): designing the screens that users actually use.
プログラム設計 (program design): designing how programming will be done based on the detailed design.
プログラミング (programming): the actual coding work.
オフショア開発 (offshore development): having development performed overseas.
ニアショア開発 (nearshore development): having development performed by other companies within the same country.
デバッグ (debugging): finding and fixing bugs.
単体テスト (unit test): プログラムやモジュールが正常に機能するかをテストする。
内部結合テスト (internal integration test): 単体で開発したプログラム同士を同一システム内で連携させて実施するテスト。
外部結合テスト (external integration test): 異なるシステム同士をつなぎ、システム間連携が問題なく行われるかをテストする。
システムテスト (system test): 定義された機能が想定どおりに実装されているかをテストする。総合テストともいう。
負荷テスト (load test): システムに高負荷をかけ、要件どおりの機能や性能となっているかをテストする。
セキュリティテスト (security test): システムがセキュリティ上問題ないかをテストする。
受入テスト (acceptance test): 構築したシステムで想定どおり業務が遂行可能かを検証するテスト。
バグ・不具合・障害: システムが想定どおりに動作しない問題を指す。
バグFIX: 不具合を修正すること。
パッチ: プログラムの変更や修正を行うためのデータ。
暫定対応: 恒久対応までの間に行う一時的な対応。
恒久対応: 暫定対応した不具合の抜本的解消を図ること。
ロールバック: システムを以前の状態に戻すこと。
システム操作マニュアル: システムの基本的な操作手順を記載したマニュアル。
業務マニュアル: 日々の業務を実施するための手順書。
トレーニング: 新業務・新システムで業務を実行するための教育。
トレーナー: トレーニングを指導する人。
移行: 業務、システム、データなどを新しい仕組みに切り替えること。
データ移行: 古いシステムから新しいシステムにデータを移動させること。
業務移行: As-Is業務を新しいTo-Be業務に移管すること。
過渡期: 新業務・新システムへの切り替え期間。
リリース（カットオーバー）: システムを本番環境にデプロイし、新しい仕組みで業務ができるようにすること。
切り戻し: 障害発生時にシステムを以前のバージョンに戻すこと。
In the requirements definition phase (要件定義フェーズ), the team finalizes the requirements definition document (要件定義書), obtains agreement from stakeholders, and hands off to the next process.

The requirements definition document should contain these elements: システム概要 (system overview), 全体像 (overall picture / landscape and configuration), WBS, 成果物一覧 (deliverables list), 業務フロー (business flows), Fit & Gap 一覧, 機能一覧 (function list), 機能要件 (functional requirements), 非機能要件 (non-functional requirements), and 業務要件 (business requirements).
システム概要: Describe the problems the system will solve based on input from business departments; this promotes a shared understanding of project goals.
全体像: System landscape and system configuration.
WBS: The work processes/phases of the system construction project.

成果物一覧: List of deliverables. Include not only what the SIer will deliver but also what the SIer expects internal SE and business departments to produce; mutually agreeing on this list prevents recognition gaps (認識齟齬).
業務フロー: As-Is/To-Be business flows. Internal SE is not responsible for creating them, but including them in the requirements document encourages business-side consideration.
Fit & Gap 一覧 (package implementations): Match business requirements against the package’s standard functions, identify gaps, then decide whether to add-on or adapt the business to the package.
機能一覧: List of functions planned for implementation.
機能要件: Requirements for screens, reports (帳票), batches, data, and interfaces.
非機能要件: Requirements for availability, operations/maintenance, security, and response time.
業務要件: Used as input to system requirements; including them as reference in the requirements document encourages business consideration.

Including business-oriented items (business flows and business requirements) in the requirements definition document, even when internal SE is not formally responsible for them, is a technique to drive business-side analysis and reduce later mismatches.

Requirements cannot be FIXed until they cover not only the scope promoted by the SIer, but also all requirements that must be driven by in-house SEs and business departments; those internal considerations must be performed and included in the requirements definition document.

Depending on SIer or in-house IT culture, the elements of requirements (as in Figure 7-9) may be compiled into a single requirements definition document, or separate documents may be created per element and the collection of those documents treated as the requirements definition document.
Rough deliverable flow: start from business flow, compile a business-requirements list, then create a requirements list from that information.
Figure 7-10 assumes multiple systems, with SIer A and SIer B each developing or modifying their assigned systems.
When building a system, functional items include screens, reports, batches, data, and interfaces; non-functional items include availability, operations/maintenance, security, and response time.
When using a system, analysis is based on the To-Be business flow (often starting from the flow assumed for the planned introduction system).
As-Is business flow is compared with To-Be business flow; differences are extracted to produce the business-requirements list and then the requirements list.
Each requirement is given a requirement number and an assigned party (e.g., Company A or Company B) so ownership across multiple SIers is explicit.
Just defining who will execute a task and by when is not a perfect score (100 points). What matters is whether all tasks have been thoroughly identified in the first place.
A deliverables list (成果物一覧) is effective for confirming the full volume of tasks. Dig deeper into RASCI and clearly assign responsibility for each deliverable, including internal company personnel.

When an SIer supports requirements definition, it is usually under a quasi-mandate contract (準委任契約) paid by work hours. Without defining who creates what in the deliverables list, time can pass vaguely without clear progress.

Use the deliverables list to align on which deliverables will be created in requirements definition and to what granularity. Aligning on what will NOT be created is equally important. Example: agreeing with the business department not to create the finest Lv3 As-Is/To-Be business flows.

Have the business department write WBS using the same template. This visualizes business-consideration tasks that become input for internal SE and prompts the business side to do proper analysis. For departments with little ownership, this can change their sense of involvement.
The deliverables list is used to align recognition of tasks among stakeholders (業務部門, internal SE, SIer).
Defining document names (ドキュメント名称) in requirements definition enables agreement on which deliverable contains which information.

System requirements definition can be consolidated into a single deliverable such as 機能要件一覧.xlsx (Functional Requirements List), covering screens, reports, batches, data, interfaces, and other requirements rather than creating separate documents for each.
Alternatively, deliverables can be split by unit (screens, reports, batches, etc.) because each element needs review during requirements definition and they are completed at different times.
Agreeing on deliverable templates (成果物のテンプレート) before work starts makes it clear who produces which deliverable, with what description, and by when, reducing recognition mismatches and omissions.
When receiving SIer support, request that they submit templates.
Example deliverable list (成果物一覧) structure: 業務フロー (As-Is/To-Be business flows at Lv1–Lv3), WBS by responsible party, 機能要件一覧, and 非機能要件一覧.
As-Is and To-Be business flows: Lv1 is the high-level flow created by the business department; Lv2 is the detailed version of Lv1; Lv3 (further detail of Lv2) is often out of scope (対象外).
WBS.xlsx (or equivalent) is produced separately for 社内SE担当, SIer担当, and 業務部門担当 work areas.
機能要件一覧.xlsx (created by SIer) covers 画面, 帳票, バッチ, データ, インターフェース, and other functional requirements.
非機能要件一覧.xlsx (created by SIer) covers 可用性, 運用保守, セキュリティ, レスポンス, and other non-functional requirements.
The kickoff meeting (キックオフ会議) is the first meeting established at the start of a project, where related stakeholders gather and it serves as the project's starting point.
First-year internal SEs (社内SE 1年生) should learn what information is communicated at the kickoff meeting and absorb the information needed to contribute.

Information typically shared at a kickoff meeting includes: the project manager's greeting, background and purpose, high-level requirements, project milestones, organization chart (体制図), and administrative information.
The purpose of system construction is not to build the system itself, but to contribute to the business; building the system is an important part but not the whole.

The project manager's greeting plus the project's background and purpose communicate which business goals are being pursued; delivering this in the manager's own words is intended to spread enthusiasm (熱量) among stakeholders.
If the project's purpose is not discussed at kickoff and system construction (the means) is spoken of as if it were the purpose, that should be judged as a danger signal.

High-level requirements (ハイレベルな要求や要件) at project kickoff communicate the project's purpose and intended means at a still-high level; an example is replacing bottleneck systems with more modern packages so that business efficiency can be raised and operations and systems can be continuously improved. A first-year in-house SE (社内SE 1年生) should not be disappointed by this lack of detail, because realizing and concretizing those high-level statements is exactly what stakeholders expect throughout the project.

Project milestones (プロジェクトマイルストーン) are the fixed destination points on the schedule. It is necessary to understand when each milestone is set and what is expected at that milestone. Preparing without that understanding can produce work far from the expected state and cause task delays. If expectations are unclear, escalate early to the project manager (or equivalent) for alignment.

From the organization chart (体制図) two things should be understood: (1) which teams form the structure and how work is divided among them, and (2) which people belong to which team. Both knowing the project members and being known by them are important. The social gathering after the kickoff meeting should be treated as an opportunity to meet as many people as possible; knowing others is essential for teamwork.

Admin-type / project-management information (アドミン系情報) such as project rules, meeting bodies (会議体), and various templates is also communicated at kickoff. A first-year in-house SE should firmly grasp these. Especially note the source/issuer of each piece of information, because it is difficult to absorb everything from a single hearing or reading and later confirmation with that person will often be needed. At the kickoff meeting, keep antennae up for who is likely to know which information.

The responsibility for creating business process flows (業務フロー) belongs to the business department. The business department must thoroughly drive business analysis so that requirements can be extracted from the flows.

In practice, internal SEs (社内SE) frequently support business-flow creation. Delayed business analysis that fails to produce requirements ultimately burdens the IT side, including internal SEs; support is therefore needed to prevent this.

Role clarification is the first support point: treat business-flow creation as the business department’s work. Align on ownership using RASCI or a deliverables list. When an SIer is contracted to assist, explicitly define the scope of that assistance.

In Fit-to-Standard package implementations, the To-Be business flow must be prepared from the package’s recommended process, not invented independently; this constraint must be understood by the business side.

The second support point is to set deadlines and actively follow progress. Even junior internal SEs should not hesitate to impose due dates, because the project is a team effort aimed at a shared business goal.
In requirements definition, roles and deadlines must be clearly defined so that the business department and internal SE can cooperate effectively.
Once roles and deadlines are set, progress can be tracked; have the business department report the status of business-flow creation in progress meetings.

Review business flows as soon as each area is finished rather than waiting until everything is complete. This lets system-requirement extraction start for finished areas and catches weak descriptions or writing-style mismatches early.

Internal SEs can provide hands-on support for As-Is business-flow creation because those flows can be produced by interviewing users about existing operations. After agreeing on deliverables with the business department, such support is acceptable (apart from the SE’s own effort).

Do not teach the business department how to write business flows. The flows become the operational design diagrams used later for user training and business improvement, so the business department itself must be able to maintain them.
If the internal SE answers writing questions even once, a lasting dependency on the SE is created. When refusal is difficult, escalate to the project manager or a supervisor.
System requirements consist of functional requirements (機能要件) and non-functional requirements (非機能要件).

Functional requirements are the functional operation requirements that users want the system to realize. Example: a function that receives customer emails and automatically registers order information from those emails into the ERP.
Non-functional requirements are requirements related to system quality other than functions, such as security and performance.

The boundary between requirements definition and basic design is often ambiguous and differs by company; some treat a completed list of system requirements as the end of requirements definition, while others include more detailed consideration of specific images of each function.
There is no single correct answer for how far requirements definition should go versus basic design, so the in-house SE should agree the scope in advance with the SIer.
Business requirements (業務要件) are distinguished from system requirements (システム要件); system requirements are further split into functional and non-functional requirements.

Figure 7-13 summarizes items that may be considered under functional requirements (機能要件). How far these items are solidified during requirements definition must be agreed with the SIer before proceeding.
A first-year in-house SE (社内SE 1年生) should not decide the scope of functional requirements alone; confirmation from the project manager is always required.

Screen requirements (画面要件) cover: screen list (画面一覧) — the list of screens the system will implement; screen transition diagram (画面遷移図) — a diagram of relationships and transitions among screens; and screen layout (画面レイアウト) — the layout of each screen.
Report requirements (帳票要件) cover: report list (帳票一覧) — the list of reports output by the system; and report layout (帳票レイアウト) — the layout of those reports.
Batch requirements (バッチ要件) cover a batch list (バッチ一覧) — the list of batches used by the system.

Data requirements (データ要件) cover: table relationship diagram (テーブル関連図) — a database design diagram; entity list (エンティティ一覧) — the list of database tables and their elements; and entity definition (エンティティ定義) — detailed definitions of those entities.

Interface requirements (インターフェース要件) cover: external system relationship diagram (外部システム関連図) — a design diagram of external linkages; interface list (インターフェース一覧) — the list of external linkages; and interface definition (インターフェース定義) — details of those linkages.
Other requirements (その他要件) include legal/statutory requirements and any functional items not covered by the categories above.

Functional requirements for a system can be identified by starting from the As-Is business flow and, from a business perspective, specifying issues that must be solved and operations that need improvement.
Scratch development can be performed using a Fit & Gap approach; Figure 7-14 shows an example applied to an order-processing (受注業務) system.

As-Is order-processing flow: orders are received by email, email contents are checked manually, orders are entered into the system by hand, and at the end of the day the number of orders is aggregated and a sales report is created in Excel. Four manual steps (①–④) consume labor.

To-Be order-processing flow: the same manual steps are automated so that the system itself performs order checking and registration, aiming at a large reduction in effort. Cases the system cannot process become exceptions that require confirmation and notification.

Concrete functions derived from the gap analysis include: ① order-content check, ② order registration, ③ registration-content confirmation plus exception notification, ④ sales-report creation and distribution, and ⑤ report-template editing.

Functional requirements (機能要件) are documented in a functional requirements list (機能要件一覧), covering features such as automatic generation of sales reports from the system, email delivery to administrators, and operations/maintenance capabilities that let business departments configure report design changes and email delivery destinations.

Functions that assume a user interface require consideration of screen requirements (画面要件). If the business department agrees that a function (e.g., registration confirmation and exception notification) can be email-only, screen requirements may be omitted.
Functions involving reports also require consideration of report/form requirements (帳票要件).
Functional requirements are further elaborated one level deeper into batch requirements (バッチ要件) and data requirements (データ要件).

Batch requirements are derived by interviewing the business department about real-time needs and processing frequencies. Example: order-content checks must run immediately after order; exception notifications every 30 minutes; sales-report delivery daily.
Data requirements are defined by listing all data that must be recorded at order time, check viewpoints/criteria, and data items to be displayed on screens and reports.
Once required data is identified, deciding where each data item comes from enables definition of interface requirements (インターフェース要件).
Example interface decisions: order data is handled via email with no other-system integration; sales-report data requires integration with the company-wide data-analysis platform.

Deepening functional requirements maps each function (order-content check, order registration, registration confirmation and exception notification, sales-report creation and delivery, report-template editing) onto the related requirement types: functional, screen, report, batch, data, and interface requirements.
System requirements and functional-requirement items have a defined relationship that is used to drive this elaboration (illustrated as 図7-15).

First-year internal SEs (社内SE) expand their contribution and raise their evaluation by accurately understanding requirements and project members' demands, but they must not stop there; they should also cultivate the habit of thinking from the customer's perspective (お客様視点).

In requirements definition (要件定義), the voices of immediate project members become the direct input. Taking those voices at face value can cause the SE to miss the issues the project truly needs to solve, resulting in business processes or systems that are inappropriate for the company's actual customers.
To avoid that outcome, internal SEs need the habit of viewing matters from the customer's standpoint and considering the real issues from that viewpoint.

Illustrative case (referencing Fig. 7-14): After functions ①–③ successfully automate previously manual work, the business department additionally plans an automatic email-reply function for order deficiencies. This would eliminate the labor of checking order contents and telephoning customers when problems are found.

The business department's perceived customer benefits are that (1) email notification lets customers correct content at a time of their choosing and (2) a link in the email body lets them jump directly to the order for immediate correction. On the surface the requirement appears unproblematic.

Customer-perspective analysis of the same requirement: the customer is in the restaurant industry and cannot sit in front of a PC all day. An email about an order deficiency would therefore often be noticed only the next morning, delaying the correction. What looks like a convenient feature internally can therefore fail to meet real customer needs.

The core question to keep asking is: “What does the customer really want?” Requirements should be examined from that customer viewpoint (even though, strictly speaking, such considerations belong in the proposal/起案 phase; the example is used here only for illustration).

When defining requirements, do not only listen to the voices of nearby stakeholders; identify the real problem from the silent customer's perspective. Example: instead of adding a post-order correction link because orders have defects, ask why customers make input mistakes in the first place.

A common root cause of order defects was mistakes in product-number entry. The better requirement is an input-assist feature that lets customers select products by photo so product-number typing is unnecessary.
Which customers you assume when analyzing problems matters. The customers in scope must be those who actually bring value to the company.

If restaurant customers are only ~10% of sales and ~90% comes from manufacturers with purchasing departments, the 'right' requirements and the picture of the problem change. Internal SE (社内SE) must identify the real customers, interpret requirements from their viewpoint, and prompt course correction when needed.

Figure 7-16 contrasts (a) the business department's heard request—email a correction link so customers fix incomplete orders themselves—with (b) the real customer issue—reduce mistakes at order time, e.g. product-number input assist—and (c) a constraint such as being able to work on a PC only in the morning so defects are not noticed immediately. Internal SE should focus on the real customer issue, not only the directly heard voice.
Non-functional requirements (非機能要件) are conditions required of a system that support the functions being implemented, rather than the functions themselves.
Examples of non-functional requirements include: screen display must complete within X seconds; reports must be output at a volume of 5,000 sheets per day.
To identify non-functional requirements, interview users about how they want each function to behave in the system, then extract those conditions as NFRs.
Key NFR categories to consider: 可用性 (Availability) — requirements for continuous usability of system services, including operation schedules and operational targets during failures.
性能、拡張性 (Performance and Scalability) — requirements on system performance and future expansion, covering future business volume and peak processing loads.
運用性、保守性 (Operability and Maintainability) — requirements on operation and maintenance services, including response levels when problems occur.
移行性 (Migratability) — requirements related to migrating from the current system, including migration period and migration targets.
セキュリティ (Security) — requirements for ensuring system safety, such as usage restrictions.
システム環境、エコロジー (System environment and Ecology) — requirements on installation environment and ecology, such as CO2 emissions.
For a new system build, all of the above non-functional requirement categories must be considered.

For modification of an existing system, most non-functional requirements are already defined; the new system's NFRs should be equal to or better than the existing system's (e.g., faster response time if the current system is slow).
Non-functional requirements of a new system are typically envisioned as equivalent to or exceeding those of the existing system.
When defining non-functional requirements (NFR), referring to the definitions of existing systems is effective and valid.
When using an existing system's NFRs as a reference, focus on systems that support the same classification of business operations.

Do not use NFRs from non-core business systems (e.g., reporting or analysis) as a reference when building a core business system (e.g., order receiving/placing or warehouse). Core-business systems tend to require higher NFR standards, while non-core systems are comparatively more relaxed.
NFRs can (and sometimes should) give rise to functional requirements. Issues discovered in NFRs may require proposals that add or change functions.

Example: A business-level requirement for master registration (assumed to be performed by an in-house SE upon request from a business department) is completion within 1 hour of the request. Even if the system itself can apply changes immediately, the 1-hour target cannot be met if many people remain in the process. To satisfy the NFR, consider a functional requirement such as an administration screen that lets users update data at a time of their choosing.

Figure 7-18 (non-functional requirements elicitation) lists example conditions: recover from failure by the next day; currently 100 users growing to 500 in 5 years; 365-day operation; existing-system data needed for the past 3 months; outsourced users must not be able to view reports; normally process 100 orders/day, with 8× volume at year-end/New Year. Associated functions include: (1) order-content check, (2) order registration, (3) registration-content confirmation and exception notification, (4) sales-report creation and distribution, (5) report-template editing.

For first-year in-house SEs (社内SE 1年生), relationships with business/operations departments that dump work require special caution; some user departments wrongly assume that after kickoff the in-house SE will independently figure out requirements and build a suitable system.

In projects initiated by business/operations departments, identifying issues and clarifying the department's WILL (how they actually want the business/operations to work) is essential; the in-house SE proposes system-based solutions, but the business/operations side—not the SE—must ultimately embed those solutions into daily work.

If a business department dumps a project so that only the in-house SE and SIer discuss it, post-go-live complaints such as 'this does not let the business run' or 'we actually wanted it this way' appear, leaving an unused system.
Junior in-house SEs often cannot yet distinguish their own proper role from what should be demanded of the business/operations department, so they may not notice they are being dumped on.
A practical countermeasure is to report one's own work regularly to a boss or project manager; if they feel discomfort that the junior is performing a given task, they can give guidance.
There will always be people who misunderstand roles; the key is managing the distance (間合い) with business/operations departments so they are not allowed to dump work.

When business/operations departments are not fulfilling their project roles, they must be made to recognize that fact. A first-year in-house SE should not directly instruct more senior people; instead, have someone the audience will listen to (supervisor, project manager, or SIer) explain what is expected of the business side.
A project is team play. You do not need to do everything yourself; if you can move the people around you and still achieve the goal, that is sufficient.

If the operations department has far too few man-hours and cannot perform adequate business consideration, consider assigning external resources such as business consultants. Users typically still have their regular work and may have little or no project experience; a supporting consultant can be effective when the expected benefit is clear.
A first-year in-house SE must never decide unilaterally to bring in external resources; the decision must be proposed to a supervisor or project manager for judgment.

People who dump work are usually neither malicious nor lazy; they simply do not know what they ought to be doing. Just as there are first-year in-house SEs, there are also first-year project members, so inclusiveness is required.

When a situation feels difficult or unpleasant, that is precisely the moment to close the distance and try to build a trusting relationship. In the author’s experience, closing the distance with the business/operations side has never felt like a failure.

There are two types of requirement omissions (要件漏れ): (1) requirements that appeared in the requirements list but were never implemented, and (2) items that were never extracted into the requirements list at all.

Requirements that are listed but not implemented may be treated as either “out of scope” (スコープ外) or as “requirement omissions” (要件漏れ). The distinction is whether stakeholders formed an explicit agreement about dropping them.

A project is assembled to achieve a shared business goal on a specific timeline. Because resources (people, materials, money, and time) are finite, the construction scope must be deliberately decided.

Choosing what to build by when is critical in system construction. Extracted requirements must be selected and discarded; the view that every listed requirement must be implemented fails to recognize that business and systems are living things.
The business environment and technology change continuously. Requirements that do not exist today may appear in a few years, months, or even days, so new requirements keep arising without end.

System construction is therefore an endless struggle: it is impossible to implement every requirement no matter how long one waits. Within a project’s time axis, teams must decide what to do and what not to do, and then pursue results against that decision.

To drive requirement omissions (要件漏れ) to zero, treat system requirements as a selection of what to include versus exclude given limited project time and budget; agreeing on that selection converts unimplemented items from omissions into out-of-scope (スコープ外) items rather than leaks.

Documentation must be paired with consensus: undocumented verbal agreements produce 'he said / she said' (言った言わない) disputes in which both sides lose (searching email history and fault-finding). Human memory fades; documents permanently record decisions.

Discussions between in-house SEs and user-department staff, no matter how detailed, do not constitute official project consensus on what will or will not be implemented. Formal agreement with the project responsible person (プロジェクト責任者) is required for the decision to be official.
Consensus with key influential leaders (キーとなるリーダー) enables the decision to be cascaded to followers.

With documented agreement: implemented requirements are in-scope (スコープ内) and unimplemented ones are out-of-scope. Without agreement: unimplemented items remain requirement omissions and implemented items are developed vaguely without a formal decision.

The essence of requirements definition is not consensus-forming alone: necessary functional requirements must be extracted as thoroughly as possible, prioritized, selected or discarded, and then implemented after agreement. If functions required to achieve the project goal are never considered or implemented, the project fails.

Basing requirements only on business flows can miss inherent/unique requirements that do not appear in the flow—such as location, language, and commercial customs. Example: overseas expansion requires checking currency, language, business customs, and statutory/legal requirements.
Business-flow-based extraction also hides frequency. A simple process judged as not worth systemizing may actually occur many times a day and be indispensable to operations.

Getting absorbed in listing requirements can produce a large list of user inconvenience-fixes. The project’s purpose is contributing to the business; re-check that listed requirements still align with the original purpose and that essential requirements have not been dropped.
Checklist to prevent missed requirements: (1) Have unique/inherent requirements been considered? (2) Has frequency been considered? (3) Can the listed requirements actually achieve the business goal?

In requirements definition (要件定義), omissions frequently occur at team boundaries or across teams. Example: one team assumes it will issue reports (帳票) for a subsequent team to work from, while the subsequent team assumes that work belongs to yet another team. Teams must jointly review requirements and premises to close these gaps.

Interfaces and coordination points with related projects are a common source of missed requirements. Example: a project plans to decommission an existing database that it no longer needs, but another project treats that same database as a prerequisite for its own system construction.

Preventing requirement extraction leaks depends on involving the right knowledgeable stakeholders (有識者). If those experts cannot participate directly, the considered content should still be reviewed by them so omissions can be caught.

In business-system development, operations and maintenance (運用保守) teams are often not involved from the requirements-definition stage, so ops/maintenance viewpoints are frequently omitted. Once requirements have somewhat come together, they should be re-checked for concerns and missing functions from an operations and maintenance perspective.

When a project involves package introduction, two perspectives are required to avoid creating individually optimal (locally optimized) systems: (1) whether the company already has a solution that implements the current requirements, and (2) whether functions the package cannot handle truly need custom or additional development.
Requirements raised in requirements definition must be properly filtered so that a globally optimal system can be designed; absorbed requirements should be checked against a defined decision logic.

Looking only at immediate requirements and focusing on how to implement them produces individually optimal mechanisms; a larger view of the company’s existing system landscape is needed to design the optimal solution.

Decision logic (Figure 7-21) for scrutinizing requirements from a globally optimal perspective includes: whether the company has an Enterprise Architect (if yes, request design support); whether a solution already implements the requirement (if yes, consider reusing already-implemented systems); whether a future IT strategy exists in the relevant domain (if yes, realize the project requirement aligned with strategy timing, accounting for timing mismatch); and whether custom development is effective or whether the business process can be changed instead.
Key terms: 個別最適 (individual/local optimization), 全体最適 (global optimization), システムランドスケープ (system landscape), エンタープライズアーキテクト (Enterprise Architect), パッケージ導入 (package introduction).

When applying requirements in a package implementation that also includes custom report creation, check the company-wide system landscape first: if reporting is already standardized via an integrated database and a common reporting tool, the package itself should not be customized for reports.
In-house junior SEs must still understand company-wide policy and functional placement of systems and evaluate requirements from that large-scale viewpoint rather than from a single project.
Custom implementation of listed requirements requires caution; fulfilling every requested item easily produces locally optimized (siloed) mechanisms.

Customization is not always wrong, but in a package-introduction project it is usually the incorrect decision because the value of a package is that the business is adapted to the package, not the reverse.

Scrutiny points for any custom requirement: (1) Can the process be changed to the package’s standard industry practice? Package functions are defined from industry-standard processes; confirm why the requirement is unique to this company versus peers.
(2) What concrete benefit is expected? Proceed only when a cost-benefit analysis shows the benefit exceeds the cost.

(3) What risk arises if the requirement is not implemented? Frequent operations whose efficiency would drop sharply may still be considered, but first debate whether the operation itself should continue; never implement merely because an influential person requested it.
(4) Will the package itself cover the need later? Legal or regulatory items may appear in a future version; check the vendor roadmap before customizing.

Screen requirements (画面要件) and form/report requirements (帳票要件) are identified by confirming with users what screens or forms they will look at while working with information output by the system, then converting those assumptions into requirements.
If the work is assumed to happen on a screen, the requirement is added to the screen list (画面一覧); if it is assumed to happen via a printed/output form, it is added to the form list (帳票一覧).
Screen requirements consist of: a screen list (the screens the system will implement), a screen transition diagram (図式 of relationships and transitions between screens), and screen layouts.
Form/report requirements consist of: a form list (the reports/forms the system will output) and form layouts.
A key question used to identify these requirements is: どんな画面や帳票で何の項目を見て作業するか？ (On what screens or forms, and looking at which items, will the user work?)

Example business functions used to drive this identification include: (1) order-content check (受注内容チェック), (2) order registration (受注登録), (3) registration-content confirmation and exception contact (登録内容確認および例外連絡), (4) sales-report creation and distribution (売上レポート作成および配信), and (5) report-template editing (レポートテンプレート編集).
These screen and form requirements are a type of functional requirement item (機能要件項目) that is solidified after understanding how users will actually operate on system outputs.
In requirements definition, screen requirements and report (帳票) requirements are identified differently for scratch development versus package introduction.
For scratch development, consider not only the screens on which users view information, but also how users reach those screens from other screens (screen transitions).
For package introduction, screens may already be implemented; in that case, identify which existing screens can be used to confirm the required information.

After identifying screen and report requirements, layouts are designed. Reports typically have company-specific definitions, so layout design is needed for both scratch development and package introduction.
Example screen set for scratch development (7 screens): login, post-login dashboard, sales detail, order detail, report edit, logout, and error.
Login, logout, and error screens may receive few user requests, but they are important and must be covered in hearings.
Screen transitions are defined by connecting identified screens with lines showing possible navigation paths.

In the sample transition diagram (Figure 7-24), login leads to the dashboard; from the dashboard users can go to order detail, sales report, and related screens; logout is reachable; an error screen can be reached from any screen.
帳票レイアウトも基本は画面と同じで、ユーザーがどのような情報をどんな帳票で見たいかを定義していく。
画面と帳票の大きな違いは、画面では情報が多い場合に下に長く表示したり改ページしたりと比較的柔軟に設計できるのに対し、帳票は紙に印刷するため表示する字数と情報量をあらかじめ決める必要がある点である。
帳票は画面のように拡大したり様々な色を用いたりできないため、使われる業務シーンをよく考えた上でフォントサイズや情報の配置場所を設計する必要がある。
社内SE 1年生が画面や帳票のレイアウトに初めて携わる場合は、フォントや文字配置の一般論を身につけるためにWebデザインの基礎を学ぶことが推奨される。
帳票テンプレートのレイアウトでは、データベースから抽出し帳票に出力される情報について、XXXや999のように何文字まで出力可能かを可視化する。
文字で表示される部分は、ユーザーの言語設定で英語に変えられる作りにする場合などもある。
日次売上レポートの帳票例では、商品コード、商品名、数量、単価、売上金額、合計などの項目と、印刷者・印刷日などのメタ情報がレイアウトされ、数値項目は桁数制限（999,999など）が明示される。

There are two types of data: master data (マスタデータ) and transaction data (トランザクションデータ). Understanding these basic concepts is necessary to organize data requirements.
Master data is fundamental information that must be configured in advance for a system to operate; the system cannot run without it.
Master data exchanged across multiple systems functions like a shared language. If master-data definitions do not match, systems cannot exchange or link information.
Transaction data is information produced as a result of using the system.
Master data defines the objects, counterparts, and business partners of a business (examples: products, customers, suppliers).
Transaction data is the historical record of business activity that is created on the basis of master data.

Manufacturing process example: R&D product information is used to identify suppliers and prepare for mass production; quotations and orders are received, goods are shipped, and invoices are issued. Transaction records are thereby generated and accumulated from the master data.

Figure 7-27 illustrates the relationship between processes and data in manufacturing: master data (R&D, product, supplier, customer) feeds subsequent transaction data (quotation, purchase order, sales order, manufacturing, shipping, invoicing, trial production, mass-production sales, make-to-order, etc.). The surrounding heading emphasizes solidifying the data flow (データフローを固める).

Data-flow principles for enterprise systems: (1) do not unnecessarily circulate process- or system-specific master data; (2) gather data that other systems will use in a single place; (3) flow required master data onward to subsequent systems.

Once data has been created inside the company and is needed by later processes or systems, collect it in one location so it can be reused. Data that is unique to a single process or system should not be circulated throughout the organization.

Example: Product information designed in R&D is integrated into ERP and then used by WMS (Warehouse Management System). In contrast, WMS-specific master data such as shipping-label print settings is process-unique and need not be treated as shared data.

Insufficient awareness of data flow causes upstream data that downstream processes actually need to remain uncirculated. Downstream users then re-enter the same data, producing inefficiency and data inconsistency.

Two diagnostic questions that prevent these errors: (1) In which system should the data a given system wants to use originally be generated? (2) Will the data generated by a given system be used by other systems?

After screen and form images are identified and layouts are defined, determine where to obtain the data for items to be displayed or printed, and extract interface requirements for information linkage between systems.
For required data items obtained from data sources (highlighted in diagrams), specify data requirements by determining exactly what data will be displayed for each item.
Confirm which system or database stores the required data, then after identifying data acquisition sources, map those data items to the system's table definitions.
Interface requirements are solidified by listing all interfaces needed for data acquisition and information linkage.
Methodology sequence for reports and forms: first define what each item on the form should display, then consider from where the data will be acquired.

Example: Daily sales report (日次売上レポート) with print items including date (年月日), report title, printer label and name, print date label and value, sequential number, product code, product name, quantity, unit price, sales amount, total label and total amount.

Print layout specifications in the sales report example include font MSP Gothic at sizes 12 or 10, digit lengths (e.g., 11 for date, 9 for product code, 12 for total amount), and alignment (left-justified for most labels and data, right-justified for amounts and some labels).
Necessary data items identified for sourcing in the sales report include date, printer name, print date, product code, product name, quantity, unit price, sales amount, and total amount.
In requirements definition, mapping is used to identify necessary data sources; those sources are then documented in an interface list (インターフェース一覧).
Figure 7-30 illustrates constructing three interfaces to retrieve data from three existing tables (e.g., system setting master, product master, and order table).
Decide the data-linkage method (batch, API, or other) and then solidify the interface requirements (インターフェース要件).
Typical interface-list columns include interface name, FROM system, TO system, and a requirements description.

Example interfaces: (1) product-master import that appropriately links updated or newly created product-master information; (2) real-time linkage of received order information; (3) linkage of processing results produced by the system under construction.

Necessary data items that must be sourced include print-related fields (date, printer name, print date, product code, product name, quantity, unit price, sales amount, total amount) plus analysis-use information.
Data sources illustrated: existing business system A (system-setting master, product master, order table) and existing analysis system B; the destination is the system being constructed.
Completing requirements definition is not sufficient if you only finish all planned meetings; you must also close (resolve) issues that were detected through discussion.
If issues are not closed, functions needed to address them may become necessary later and bounce back as additional requirements.
Issues vary: some must be resolved during requirements definition, while others can be left to subsequent phases without problem. First agree on which issues need to be solved now, then close them.
Classify issues into those that must be solved during requirements definition versus those that can be solved after it. Further classify by whether the cause of the issue is already known.
For issues whose cause is known: confirm the actions needed for resolution and follow through on them.
For issues whose cause is unknown: check whether ownership is adequate, whether subject-matter experts are involved, whether deadlines are set, and whether follow-up meeting structures exist.

If it is unclear who should be involved to solve an issue, escalate to the project manager and obtain support. Issues do not have to be solved by one person; the team should work together to move the project forward.
Process for issue closing: identify remaining issues and prompt action → resolve issues → proceed to requirements FIX (finalization).
When root-cause analysis is not progressing, ask: Is appropriate ownership missing? Are experts insufficient? Are deadlines set? Is there a meeting body for follow-up?
Before resolving issues in requirements definition, first confirm that appropriate discussions are actually progressing and that issues have been sufficiently identified (aburi-dasarete iru).

Three methods to confirm the progress of consideration (kentou no susumi-guai): (1) Check whether planned meetings are being held/completed as scheduled. If discussions are not advancing in those meetings, consideration is not advancing. Causes include insufficient preparation, overly optimistic initial plans, or delays from unforeseen events, all of which require response.

(2) Check deliverables. Defining in a deliverable list (seika-butsu ichiran) which artifacts will be produced, to what level of granularity, and by when makes progress visible (referenced from p.164).
(3) Infer progress from the volume and nature of issues recorded in the issue management table (kadai kanri-hyou, p.76).

Issue-count trend as a progress signal (Figure 7-33: kadai-suu to zan-kadai-suu no suii): Phase ① (early requirements definition) shows few detected issues, mostly administrative (meetings not set, unclear deliverables). Phase ② shows a rise in issue count; this feels like a problem but is actually healthy evidence that consideration is advancing, and issue content shifts toward process, system, and data topics. Phase ③ indicates planned meetings have been completed and consideration has progressed substantially. If issues are then closed normally, remaining issues decline toward resolution (phase ④).

The overall technique is titled 'Confirming hard-to-see progress' (mie-nikui shinchoku wo kakunin suru): using meetings, deliverables, and issue-occurrence patterns as proxies when conventional progress is not directly visible.

In requirements definition (要件定義), the last crucial task is to properly FIX the requirements. Requirements do not become fixed automatically; the in-house SE (社内SE) must make them get fixed by acting proactively.
Core principle: requirements are not something you FIX yourself, but something you MAKE get FIXed (要件はFIX“する”ではなく“させる”).
The in-house SE must take initiative on three actions to force requirements to FIX: documenting (文書化), identifying the responsible person (責任者の特定), and setting the venue/occasion (場の設定).

Documenting: human memory is extremely ambiguous. Content decided in requirements definition must be documented (or made to be documented) so decisions remain. Anything not written on paper is equivalent to not existing, which is a loss for the in-house SE. Always document.

Identifying who must agree: the people who discuss/consider requirements and the people who bear responsibility are different. Requirements are confirmed only when agreement is reached with the person who is the responsible party on the organizational chart (体制図).
Key insight for solidifying requirements: it is not what you agree on that matters most, but who you agree with.

In some projects, people who do not appear on the organizational chart still hold strong speaking rights and influence (e.g., the president of a local subsidiary). These stakeholders must be taken into account when fixing requirements.
Even as a first-year in-house SE (社内SE) for whom identifying certain stakeholders may be difficult, it is important to share requirements with those people as well.

A venue for agreement (合意する場) is important: involve both the person responsible and other appropriate people who are not the responsible party so that consensus can be formed and made official. If people you want to involve cannot attend, you must distribute information about the decisions.

Requirements FIX (要件のFIX) is like deciding a cross-section and boldly cutting it off. As long as the business grows and operations keep changing, system modification requests never end, so priorities must be set and a decision made on which requirements this project will build now.

The purpose of requirements FIX is not to solidify the development target. It is to share the business goals the project wants to achieve on its timeline. If sufficient business consideration has not progressed or system requirements are not complete, the FIX should be postponed.

Postponing a requirements FIX requires considerable courage for a first-year in-house SE and is difficult. Escalating to a project manager may result in them forcing requirements to be solidified anyway; that is the project manager’s problem, and the in-house SE should still take the correct action.

After requirements FIX, system development and business design (e.g., user training) proceed toward the agreed vision. Subsequent chapters cover how to proceed after basic design from the in-house SE perspective.
There is an explicit concept of “FIXしない判断” (the judgment not to FIX/freeze requirements) when conditions for a proper freeze are not met.
When gathering requirements, do not only listen to the business departments present; also consider issues from the perspective of customers who are not in the room.
Map requirements against the company's overall system landscape so that project-level responses do not produce local optima that harm the wider architecture.
Document requirements and then FIX them by obtaining agreement from the right people in the right forum.
Use a deliverables list to agree who will produce each artifact; this prevents omitted work and misaligned understanding.
Every project has requirements that will not be addressed. Proper consensus-building turns those items into explicit out-of-scope decisions rather than requirement omissions.
Completing every scheduled meeting is not enough: if issues that must be resolved during requirements definition remain open, the risk of requirement leakage remains.

Requirements-definition approach differs by whether the system is being built or used. For build: the gap between As-Is and To-Be business flows becomes the system requirements. For use: work from already-defined business flows.
After requirements are successfully fixed (FIX), development cannot simply be left entirely to the contracted SIer; the internal (in-house) SE must continue to lead and stay involved.

A well-known satire cartoon of system development projects, based on an experiment at the University of Oregon and titled around “what the customer really needed,” illustrates how handing everything off (“丸投げ”) produces a mismatch with actual needs.

The cartoon contrasts successive interpretations: the requirements the customer requested, the project leader’s interpretation, the analyst’s design, the programmer’s code, the implemented system, and finally what the customer actually needed—showing differences in how each party grasps the same request.
When an SIer performs development, the in-house SE still has a defined leadership and oversight role rather than a hands-off stance.
SIer test results require specific caution and review rather than uncritical acceptance.
Training support after implementation has mandatory activities that the customer/in-house side must still perform.
Chapter framing: these issues (in-house SE role during SIer development, scrutiny of SIer tests, and required training support) are the questions the chapter is intended to resolve.

A satirical cartoon (Figure 8-2) illustrates a common project failure pattern: the customer's requested requirements already diverge from what they actually needed; those requests are then interpreted differently by the project leader, analyst, and programmers. The result is no usable deliverables, high cost, and a system that cannot be operated.

Even after requirements are formally fixed (FIX), complacency is dangerous. If how the system is built is not actively followed, the SIer may complete it according to its own arbitrary interpretation.
The in-house SE (社内SE) must therefore guide system construction toward the proper intended form rather than leaving interpretation solely to the vendor.
Chapter 8 assumes waterfall development supported by an SIer and covers key points from basic design through unit-test and integration-test result reviews.

Typical role split in this phase: SIer performs basic design, detailed design, coding, unit testing, integration testing, system testing, and acceptance-test support; the in-house SE reviews the basic design document, reviews unit/integration test results, reviews plans and results, participates in system testing and acceptance-test support, manages progress, and supports training preparation; the business department prepares and delivers training and conducts acceptance testing.
When constructing a system with SIer support, the in-house SE (社内SE) aims to guarantee system quality by managing progress and outputs rather than developing directly.
Typical flow with SIer support: SIer writes design documents → in-house SE reviews them → SIer develops and tests based on the reviewed content → in-house SE reviews the test results.
Because the in-house SE does not participate directly in development, the quality of design documents and the related process guarantees become the key.
Progress management presupposes prior agreement with the SIer on requirements and the list of deliverables (成果物一覧); only then is progress managed.

Progress management is a repeating cycle of mechanism setup → information collection → judgment → action. These must be run as one set. Creating only the mechanism, only collecting information, only judging, or only acting (action without follow-through) is NG.
進捗管理を実施し、適切な情報が適切なタイミングで社内SEに集まり、判断と行動ができる状態にする必要がある。そのために、まずは進捗管理の仕組みを作る必要がある。
進捗管理の仕組みの一つは「進捗報告会をセッティングする」こと。日次、週次、月次など定期的な進捗・課題確認の場を設定する。定期的に確認しなければ進捗や課題の情報を収集できない。
進捗管理の仕組みの一つは「ツールを導入する」こと。ツールやフォーマットを導入し、進捗の可視化を行う。自社にツールがない場合は、SIerがプロジェクトで常用する進捗管理ツールを使わせてもらうのも手である。
進捗管理の仕組みの一つは「報告フォーマットを用意する」こと。小規模プロジェクトであればWBSを見ながら進捗やうまくいっていないことを共有することも可能だが、関係者が多い場合は進捗状況、課題、打ち手、次週の予定などを整理する文書化が必要。筆者はPowerPointを使うことが多い。
進捗管理の流れ（図8-4）: 要件FIX・開発対象の合意 → 成果物一覧・予定の合意 → 進捗管理の仕組み作り。その後、判断・情報収集・行動依頼/行動のサイクルを回す。
図8-5は「進捗管理の1セット」として、進捗管理のための仕組み（報告会、ツール、報告フォーマット）を示している。
The purpose of receiving progress reports (進捗報告) is not mere information collection. It is to gather necessary information, make judgments, and prompt action (or take action yourself).

If a company's business/operations departments and an SIer could successfully build systems without problems, the occupation of in-house SE (社内SE) would not exist. In-house SEs exist because those parties alone encounter difficulties that must be handled.

Projects do not proceed simply by making a plan and executing it; they proceed by uncovering issues and resolving them as they go. Forgetting this and dumping everything onto others (丸投げ) will fail because of the nature of projects.
Progress-report formats differ by project, but the viewpoints you need to collect are the same.
Key progress-report viewpoint — current progress: how actual work status compares to the plan.
Key progress-report viewpoint — discovered issues and response status: what issues have been found and how they are being resolved.
Key progress-report viewpoint — next week's schedule: next week's activities and whether preparation for them is on track. Sharing this across teams enables outreach to related teams.

Key progress-report viewpoint — other reports and concerns: items that may seem unrelated to the project (e.g., a team member taking long leave) are still very important for risk identification (リスク吸い上げ).
Progress reports should be received in a progress-report meeting (進捗報告会) so the in-house SE can judge and act, not just collect status.

When a junior in-house SE receives a progress report and collects information, they often still struggle with what next action to take; Figure 8-7 summarizes attention points for detecting issues from progress reports and converting them into follow-up actions.
Progress deviation (予定と実績の乖離): There is always a cause for plan-vs-actual gaps; dig into whether the delay cause is temporary or recurring, and whether countermeasures exist if it will recur.

Zero issues (課題ゼロ) is impossible in a real project; absence of issues should raise suspicion that necessary analysis has not been done. Review deliverables even in intermediate form, because 'no issues' often means work items have not been identified (洗い出せていない).

Issue stagnation (課題滞留): Issues are raised but never closed, which often means the right people have not been involved. Inventory the issues and define who can resolve each one and how; never try to solve every issue on the spot.

Missing progress reports: Possible causes include reporters only covering what is going well and omitting uncomfortable topics, or coordination gaps that leave some work outside the reporting scope (especially in complex multi-SIer setups). Prevent this by using the organization chart or RASCI to set reporting coverage, or by keeping project structure simpler.
Who reports matters: When both veterans and beginners are on the project, listen more carefully to beginners' progress reports.
Key terms preserved: RASCI (responsibility matrix), SIer (system integrator), 進捗報告 (progress report), 課題 (issues/risks), 体制図 (organization chart).

To succeed at basic design, do not fully outsource (丸投げ) basic design to the SIer; properly review deliverables. People who do not understand 丸投げ may believe they are acting correctly while actually having dumped the work.

丸投げ is not only doing nothing and abandoning the project. If you merely think you are acting but cannot course-correct toward the right direction, the result is the same as 丸投げ to the SIer: high invoices, no deliverables, and operations that do not run.
Pattern of 丸投げ in-house SE: not knowing what deliverables exist or when they will be completed. Without that grasp you cannot notice delays or that the SIer skipped considering countermeasures.

Pattern of 丸投げ in-house SE: not attending meetings or not speaking. Leaving meetings entirely to the business department and SIer is 丸投げ and prevents guiding the system in the right direction. Attending but staying silent when you should speak can be worse than absence, because the in-house SE’s presence may be treated as agreement and become a fait accompli.
Pattern of 丸投げ in-house SE: not thinking for yourself. Even if an experienced SIer presents plausible opinions, uncritically accepting them without comment is 丸投げ.
Core practice associated with this rule: review the basic design documents (基本設計書をレビューする).
A true in-house SE (社内SE) is an IT-department person who understands the company's own business and operations and can think about matters from the company's standpoint.
When reviewing a basic design document (基本設計書), system-specific technical content differs by project; reviewers should therefore focus on the cross-cutting points summarized in Figure 8-8.

Requirements viewpoint: Even if requirements were thought to have been conveyed correctly, a different interpretation by the person writing the basic design will send system design in the wrong direction. Review must confirm not only that requirements are implemented but also that the design actually solves the business problems; the requirements themselves may be wrong, and this is best discovered before implementation.

Information quantity and quality: A design document is adequate only if a programmer can construct the required system from it. Documents that programmers cannot understand are NG. Information that is common sense to SIers who participated in requirements definition may be unknown to programmers.

Authorship: Besides what is written, who wrote the document matters. Individual personality appears in design-document descriptions, and quality differences between a 10-year SIer veteran and a first-year engineer are to be expected.

Horizontal expansion of issues (問題点の横展開): When a problem is found in one design document, similar corrections are usually needed in other specifications. The SIer should be asked to propagate the finding across deliverables so that the same comment need not be repeated multiple times.

Company-wide system picture: An SIer's basic design covers only the project scope. Reviewers must still ask 'how does this fit the company's systems as a whole?' For example, aligning a new UI with existing internal UIs reduces user learning cost.
Involving internal experts: Have in-house specialists (infrastructure, operations, security, etc.) review the relevant portions of the basic design and provide advice.
Involving business departments: Have business units review selected parts of the basic design as needed. Although IT and business have distinct roles, they should cooperate to guarantee quality.

Key statement: 「自社ビジネスと業務を理解し、自社の立場で物事を考えられるIT部門の人間が本来の社内SEです。」 (The genuine in-house SE is an IT-department person who understands the company's business and operations and can think from the company's standpoint.)

In system construction, testing is performed in stages by people with different roles (SIer, IT department, business department, etc.) to guarantee quality; all viewpoints are not checked in a single test.
If an in-house SE does not understand each test type’s viewpoint, they may make off-the-mark comments, such as asking why an SIer’s unit-test report lacks business-scene scenarios.

Testing proceeds from the small to the large: first confirm developed details (modules), then connections among multiple modules, then overall system quality, and finally whether the system whose operation has been verified actually meets business requirements.

In V-shaped waterfall development, test types map to development phases and scopes as follows: unit testing (単体テスト) ↔ detailed design, module-unit scope; integration testing (結合テスト) ↔ basic design, multiple modules; system testing (システムテスト) ↔ requirements definition, entire system; acceptance testing (受入テスト) ↔ requirements analysis, a series of business operations.
The V-model correspondence is: programming under detailed design (unit test), basic design (integration test), requirements definition (system test), and requirements analysis (acceptance test).
Who conducts software tests depends on project scale and how SIers (System Integrators) are organized.
In a relatively small project developed by a single SIer, the SIer typically performs system testing, after which internal SE and the business department perform acceptance testing.

When multiple SIers develop the system, the internal SE performs system testing that combines SIer A’s and SIer B’s systems (sometimes called 総合テスト / comprehensive testing); the business department then performs acceptance testing.
Depending on the contract, SIers may support internal-SE system testing that spans multiple systems.
Typical test-scope image: unit tests (単体テスト) cover individual modules; integration tests (結合テスト) cover combinations of modules/functions; system tests (システムテスト) cover the overall assembled system.
Role-division example (single SIer, small project): SIer owns unit/integration and system tests; internal SE and business department own acceptance tests.
Role-division example (multiple SIers, medium project): each SIer owns its own unit/integration tests; internal SE owns combined system testing; business department owns acceptance testing.
Unit-test and integration-test result reviews are used to confirm that development proceeded as planned; the earlier defects and failures are found, the more time and leeway remain for fixes.
Three review viewpoints for unit-test and integration-test results: (1) tests were planned appropriately, (2) tests were executed correctly, and (3) defects were properly fixed.

Confirming that tests were planned appropriately: reviewing only results is insufficient; the validity of the original test plan must also be checked. For unit tests in scratch development, test validity can be assessed via test density (number of tests ÷ system development scale). Each SIer typically has test-density criteria; check whether results meet those criteria, and if not, whether the reasons for falling short are valid.
Confirming that tests were executed correctly uses bug density, calculated as number of bugs ÷ system development scale.
Bug-density example (both programs 1,000 lines): development ① found 10 defects → bug density 0.01; development ② found 100 defects → bug density 0.1. Development ② is clearly of worse quality.
Bug-density example with different scale: development ③ of 10,000 lines found 100 defects → bug density 0.01 (same density as the 1,000-line case with 10 defects).
Even if the number of bugs is highest in case ③, quality can still be considered equivalent to case ①.
Bug density can be examined overall, but it should also be verified by developed function. For function areas with abnormally high bug density, deep-dive into why only that area has high bug density.
Defects detected in testing must be thoroughly and completely fixed; that is where the meaning lies.
From the trends of detected defects (visible issues), it becomes possible to catch potential/latent problems and uncover yet-undetected defects in advance.

Viewpoints/hints for discovering latent problems from detected defects: What are the trends of detected defects? Are defects concentrated/biased toward some functions? Is there any sense of incongruity in the locations where defects were detected? Are defects appearing in places where they ought to appear, and does this match development difficulty? Are there locations where defects occurred even though they were simple modification spots? Are there locations where no defects were detected at all? Was the testing planned with sufficient quality and quantity in the first place? If these results were reported to the project manager/project leader, what kinds of questions would likely be asked?

Actions to take based on test results (considering bug density vs. test density): When bug density is high due to insufficient test density, analyze the cause of many bugs and request additional tests. When high bugs may indicate that testing was insufficient from the start, analyze causes and request additional tests. Additional action may not be needed in other cases (e.g., low bug density).
A completed system that cannot actually be used is a wasted asset (宝の持ち腐れ). Training must be delivered and post-release operations must be supported.
Two kinds of training exist: basic-operation training based on the system operation manual, and business-operation training based on the business manual.
Basic-operation training teaches fundamental system usage following the system operation manual.
Business-operation training teaches the end-to-end business flow that uses the system, following real operational procedures and processes.
The internal SE (社内SE) is responsible only for basic system-operation training; business-operation training is the responsibility of the business department (業務部門).

The internal SE does not write business manuals. Even when the business department needs screenshots or basic-operation information for its materials, the business department remains the owner of business training.
Roles: business staff and the business department own business-flow and business-manual training; the internal SE owns the operation-manual / basic-operation training.

Internal SEs (社内SE) must obtain necessary information from the business department (業務部門) and support training preparation, regardless of whether business staff create detailed plans and conduct training themselves (especially common in small projects).

Training period and timing: Packaged software or SaaS typically allow relatively flexible training-environment setup; scratch development often requires coordination between development and training environments. Training requested too early may occur before functions are implemented or quality is guaranteed, risking the need for retraining—this should be communicated to the business department.

Training scenarios: Training frequently runs in parallel with development and testing. Even if the application is ready, data required to use the system may not yet be prepared. Hear from the business department what training they envision and determine who will prepare the necessary data by when.

Training evaluation criteria: Responsibility for training business users and ensuring proficiency rests with the business department. Training without proficiency metrics or criteria risks being incomplete (“やりっぱなし”), which can surface as operational failure after go-live and trigger rushed feature additions. A mechanism to measure training proficiency is required.
If the business department lacks sufficient effort or motivation for training, the resulting system may go unused. When budget allows, an SIer can be engaged to support training.
Traditional system development mainly used Fit & Gap: systems were developed or customized to match existing business operations.
In recent years Fit to Standard has become mainstream: fully utilize packages/services together with best practices and remain able to adopt version upgrades.
