Fit to Standard requires fitting the business to the system, which means changing not only processes but also people’s thinking and ways of working; the management method for that is change management (チェンジマネジメント).
First-year in-house SEs (社内SE 1年生) are advised to grasp three key points about change management.

Change management sits at the intersection of a new system, new strategy, and new business, driving the shift from traditional thinking, values, and ways of working to new thinking, values, and ways of working by executing change and reform (変更・改革実行).
Figure 8-15 illustrates change-management involvement: new system / new strategy / new business versus conventional vs. new mindsets, values, and work styles.

In change management, change is intentionally planned and executed, with various information sent through various means; first-year in-house SEs (社内SE) must consciously receive information by considering when, where, who, how, and what change is expected.

Information dissemination channels include regular email distribution, Web, meetings, and drinking parties; it is necessary to understand why a particular channel, person, and wording was chosen rather than letting information pass through unexamined.
From the first year as an in-house SE, a habit is required of not letting information pass by and instead thinking about the intent (狙い) of the information.

A first-year in-house SE almost never bears the entirety of change management (チェンジマネジメント); a dedicated team typically handles organization/project-level work, which the individual then personalizes (自分事化) into their own responsibilities.
Even when change is aimed at the entire organization, it will not occur unless it ultimately connects to change at the team-unit and individual-unit levels.

After personalizing the change, the wave of change originating from the project must be propagated to the organization, team, and stakeholders; even a first-year in-house SE must take on the role of propagating the message.

Organization/project-level change management includes: clarifying vision, purpose, and issues; building a change system; disseminating information to employees; preparing the change environment and addressing inhibiting factors; and setting short- and long-term goals with evaluation.

Individual-level actions (including in-house SEs) include: personalizing issues (課題の自分事化); understanding one's contribution in the assigned area; information dissemination and exchange within the team; addressing inhibiting factors; and understanding goals.
The core framework is to personalize overall change management and connect it to action (自分事化して行動に結びつける).
Project transformation does not become an overall movement unless it ultimately connects to individual-level change.
Whenever change is being promoted, opposition that refuses and will not accept the change almost always appears.
Typical project composition regarding change: about 10–20% are motivated leaders, about 10–20% are opposition, and the remainder are followers who neither lead nor oppose.
This 10–20% / 10–20% / rest ratio is roughly the same regardless of project size.
A better interpretation of opposition is not people who intentionally sabotage, but people who take a bit more time and effort than others to accept new ways of working and thinking.
Assume a certain number of opponents will always exist, and ease up rather than treating them as an unexpected threat.
Rule: opposition to the project always appears; understand the nature of that opposition.
Figure 8-17 (types regarding change): 1–2割 leaders, 1–2割 opposition, others followers.
Jeanie Duck of the Boston Consulting Group named people uncooperative with organizational change as "Change Monsters" and classified them into seven types.
タコツボドン (Takotsubo-don): Like an octopus hiding in a pot, this type does not try to form connections with others.
ウチムキング (Uchimukingu): Has an inward-looking perspective and only values internal company evaluations.
カコボウレイ (Kakoborei): Turns away from the present situation and clings to the past.
ミザル・イワザル・キカザル (Mizaru-Iwasaru-Kikazaru): Adopts a "none of my business" attitude and waits for the storm of reform to pass.
ノラクラ (Norakura): Only lists negative opinions and excuses and does not cooperate with reform.
マンテン (Manten): Aims for a perfect score and therefore will not take action if there is any risk.
カイケツゼロ (Kaiketsu-zero): Skilled at pointing out problems and making excuses but unable to produce solutions.
The countermeasure is the same regardless of opposing-force type: first try to communicate the necessary message yourself; if that fails, pass the baton to the next person.
Opposing forces tend to place more weight on "who" is speaking than on "what" is being said.
If personal persuasion fails, escalate so that others handle the interaction; continue climbing the organizational chart as needed and pursue a team solution rather than handling it alone.

The identical message delivered by a different person can sometimes succeed in persuasion—possibly because the listener attends to rank rather than the individual, because repeated exposure from multiple sources produces acceptance, or simply because of timing. Multi-person persuasion often works surprisingly well.
People in the opposing camp are fundamentally good; do not take an adversarial stance. Approach with an open mind, stand beside them, and speak toward the proper goal rather than at the person.
To start testing or training in a system construction project, the application, data, infrastructure, and physical business environment must all be in place.

Ideally, requirements needed for testing and training should be identified in the contract with the SIer at project start. When the contract is signed before system requirements and To-Be business flows are finalized, test/training requirements should be organized once functional and non-functional requirements have solidified to some degree.

Conduct hearings with business departments on testing and training, then coordinate with the SIer based on those results. Not every condition must be accepted: clarify what is and is not possible in consultation with the SIer, and also adjust with the business departments.
Four environments commonly appear in system construction projects: production (本番環境), development (開発環境), verification (検証環境), and training (トレーニング環境).
Production environment (本番環境): the environment in which daily operations are performed after business-department acceptance testing is complete.
Development environment (開発環境): the environment used for system development; after go-live it is still used for bug-fix program changes and enhancement development.
Verification environment (検証環境): the environment used for unit testing, integration testing, and later test stages; after go-live it is used to confirm modified applications.
Training environment (トレーニング環境): the environment in which users train; after system release it continues to be used as a dedicated training environment.
When preparing verification environments (検証環境) and training environments (トレーニング環境), decide whether to use the same environment or separate ones based on which factors matter most for the project.

Same environment for verification and training: construction can be done once; maintenance costs can be kept down; testing and training require coordination, and there is a risk of training delays if a failure occurs.

Separate environments for verification and training: construction must be performed multiple times (including data-loading effort, not just build cost); maintenance costs are higher; testing and training can each be done at independent, arbitrary times.

Data must be loaded into verification/training environments because applications will not run without master settings. Agree in advance with the business department on who prepares the data and how; internal SEs often assume it is the business side’s job while the business side assumes it is the SE’s job.

Testing/training may also require surrounding systems used in preceding or following processes. Some organizations have constraints that prevent data linkages from being established in the verification/training environment. Identify the full list of required systems from the test/training scope and prepare working inter-system connections.
The purpose of receiving progress reports is to gather necessary information, identify problem areas, and prompt action (or take action yourself).
In testing, the earlier a defect is noticed (in an earlier process), the more time can be secured for fixes; the later the process, the higher the risk of release delay.

In package implementation, Fit to Standard is mainstream: leverage best practices and align business to the system. Change management is the method for managing changes in thinking and ways of working.
In basic design, manage the SIer's process (progress) and output (deliverables) to guarantee quality.
Testing uses various types of tests conducted in stages by people with different roles; a single test does not guarantee everything.
Conduct training to prepare for release. Training has two types: learning basic operations, and learning business operations using the system.
Even if requirements are FIX'd, throwing everything over is forbidden. If the internal SE does not follow up, there is a risk of producing a system that diverges from the intended system.
Chapter 9 covers testing after unit and integration testing. In many cases, in-house SEs (社内SE) lead system testing, after which business or operations departments conduct acceptance testing.
Defects found in system testing should not be viewed as purely negative. Any system construction will produce defects to some degree.
A project's purpose is not to build a perfect system, but to create business operations that achieve the intended effects; the system is only one element of that.
Defects detected during testing are an opportunity to raise quality before release. The worst outcome is failing to detect defects, which then become production incidents.
Defects found in testing are important for preventing production failures. They are not bad; they are chances for quality improvement and should be actively found and fixed before release.

Key questions addressed in the chapter: how to correctly view testing defects for quality improvement; the difference between system testing and acceptance testing; what to prepare for system testing; and what system testing should guarantee.

System testing (システムテスト) is a critical checkpoint that determines whether a system built by an SIer (system integrator) will be accepted; it guarantees system quality and connects to acceptance testing by business departments.

System testing confirms that functions defined based on functional requirements have been implemented as expected. The internal SE (社内SE) is responsible for this system-perspective verification of functional and non-functional requirements, not for business-perspective testing.

If functions are implemented exactly as specified in the requirements but actual operations cannot support the intended business after go-live, that outcome is not directly the internal SE's responsibility. The internal SE's role is to confirm from a system viewpoint that requirements were implemented as designed.

The above division of responsibility is an extreme interpretation. Future internal SEs are expected not only to deliver systems that match specifications but also to contribute to the business by crossing departmental boundaries.

System testing is an umbrella term covering various tests. In practice its definition varies by company and SIer: it may mean only functional testing, or it may encompass all of the tests shown in Figure 9-2.
Within the broad framework of system testing, individual test types (as in Figure 9-2) may be executed separately, or a single broad system test may incorporate elements of those various tests.

How system testing is planned and executed depends on company culture and the SIer, so confirmation is required. Even when the test categories are sliced differently, the underlying elements used to raise system quality remain largely the same.
System testing (システムテスト) includes several representative types, as shown in Figure 9-2 of Chapter 9.

システム間連携テスト (外部結合テスト / inter-system linkage test / external integration test): Confirms there are no problems with interfaces between the new system and systems it collaborates with. Although already performed in integration testing, it may be reconfirmed before system testing. Especially when a verification environment is shared internally, communication that worked in integration testing can later fail due to external influences.

機能テスト (functional test): Confirms the functions users require as agreed in the requirements definition. Often conducted together with performance tests and load tests. Scenarios are created from functional requirements and then executed.

性能テスト (performance test): Confirms system response performance and data processing speed as defined in non-functional requirements. Typically performed late in testing, once a certain quality level is assured, in verification or production environments.

ユーザビリティテスト (usability test): Confirms whether the system is easy for users to use. Because usability can also be observed during functional and performance tests, it is sometimes integrated with those tests.

セキュリティテスト (security test): Confirms that security requirements agreed in the requirements definition are met. In business companies, security requirements are often defined by infrastructure or security teams, which also often execute the tests.

リグレッションテスト (回帰テスト / regression test): Used in additional development to confirm that existing functions that were not modified still work correctly. Full coverage of all functions is impractical, so testing focuses on processes and data that could be indirectly affected.

負荷テスト (load test): Functional tests that check behavior are normally run without load. Real operations can involve many simultaneous users or concentrated orders that create high load, so load tests are executed based on non-functional requirements.
現新比較テスト (current-vs-new comparison test): Used when replacing an existing system. Data output by the old system is compared with data output by the new system to confirm there are no problems.
The system testing process can be broadly classified into two parts: planning (計画) and execution/implementation (実施).
The greatest enemy in system testing is not the defects discovered during testing, but time itself. Limited test time is the primary constraint.
To make time an ally, effectively use the relatively flexible period before testing starts to create the system test plan.
A good system test plan not only prepares the required content properly, but also considers the arrangements (段取り) for making effective use of pre-test time.

Related system testing deliverables include: test plan documents (テスト計画書), test procedure documents (テスト手順書), start/end judgment checklists (開始・終了判定チェックリスト), methods for leaving evidence (エビデンスの残し方), and progress management tools (進捗管理ツール).
Start preparing these artifacts as early as possible rather than waiting until testing begins.
It is not necessary to create everything from scratch; contact people who worked on past projects and reuse existing materials.
Key principle (quote): 「システムテストにおける最大の敵は、システムテストで発見される不具合ではなく、時間です。」— The biggest enemy in system testing is not the bugs found during system testing, but time.
When preparing for system testing, research past in-house resources and actively reuse whatever can be reused to advance preparation.

System-test-related deliverables (システムテスト関連成果物) include: test plan, start/end judgment checklist, test scenario list, test procedure document, evidence, progress/issue management table (or tool), and test result summary.

テスト計画書 (test plan): documents the purpose, premises, scope, procedures, schedule, and organization of the test. Creating the plan both refines test preparation and enables information sharing among stakeholders.

開始・終了判定チェックリスト (start/end judgment checklist): a pre-compiled list of items needed to decide whether testing may start or end. Preparing it in advance enables comprehensive, calm judgment that is not swayed by the atmosphere of the moment; it can also serve as source material for internal reports.

テストシナリオ一覧 (test scenario list): exhaustively enumerate conceivable test scenarios without first deciding which will be executed; then use the list to select which scenarios will be performed and which will not.
テスト手順書 (test procedure document): records the detailed test steps for each scenario that has been selected for execution from the scenario list.
エビデンス (evidence): artifacts that prove tests were executed accurately; when defects occur they become input for sharing the issues with the SIer (system integrator) or other parties.
進捗・課題管理表（ツール） (progress/issue management table or tool): Excel sheets or other tools used to track test progress and issues; the company may mandate a particular tool.

テスト結果サマリー (test result summary): records planned versus actual test counts, discovered defects, and repaired defects, and also organizes issues identified from defect trends. It is recommended not only for reporting but also as material for reflecting on the system test itself.
System testing (システムテスト) is driven by the system test plan document (システムテスト計画書), so the plan must be carefully developed with sufficient time.
A system test plan should cover at least: purpose of testing (テストの目的), scope (範囲/スコープ), and how testing will proceed (テストの進め方), including process and role assignment.

Purpose of testing: clearly state what the system test is meant to guarantee; purpose then determines test range and premises. Example: for a minor functional change, exclude performance and guarantee only the defined functions.
Scope: state which areas are in range. Scope can be cut by system, data, business, functions, etc.; project agreement on scope is mandatory.
Data-scope example: which master data is assumed as a premise, and how much data from the system being replaced will be migrated into the test environment.
Function-scope example: if 100 functions were planned but only 80 are finished due to delay, treat the 80 as phase 1 and the rest as phase 2.
How to proceed: document two things—the overall arrangement/process (段取り) and role assignment (役割分担).

Role-assignment examples: in-house SE writes test scenarios and executes them with the SIer; SIer runs performance tests while in-house SE reviews scenarios and confirms results; infrastructure team leads security tests.
System test schedules should describe the overall timeline, including specific dates for when the test scenario list is created and by when test procedure documents must be created from that list.

A test schedule must also account for time after testing for the SIer to fix defects and for the in-house SE to re-test those fixes. Failing to plan this time can leave insufficient room for fixes or make the project appear delayed.
The duration needed for defect fixes varies with project scale and development difficulty and typically requires experience to estimate. If estimation is difficult, consult the project manager.
Test organization (テスト体制) should clearly define who plays which roles based on the contract. In small projects one person may hold multiple roles.

Example system-test roles: テスト推進 (overall management); テスト実施 (execute assigned scenarios and raise/report defects); 障害管理 (track reported defects in a list or tool); 障害解消確認 (quality-check fixed applications); 報告資料作成 (prepare materials to communicate test results); テスト環境用意 (prepare the test environment).
Admin-related information should also be recorded: storage locations for test-related documents, and decisions made in team meetings or other communications.

System tests (shown in Figure 9-2 on page 225) may be planned and executed as dedicated tests or conducted within broader system testing; in either case, start with inter-system linkage testing (システム間連携テスト / 外部結合テスト) to guarantee data linkage between systems.

Preceding and following business processes require data linkage between systems. An SIer guarantees integration among modules inside the system they built, so inter-system linkage testing is performed by the in-house SE (社内SE) from that point onward (the SIer may assist depending on the contract).

System defects arise from recognition discrepancies (認識齟齬). These discrepancies readily occur at 'gaps' (はざま): between people, between one's own team and another team, and between one's own company and another company.

Inter-system linkage testing sits exactly at such a gap and is therefore a high-risk point for defects; it must be approached carefully. Raising the quality of inter-system linkage at this stage allows subsequent tests to proceed more efficiently and effectively.

The source for inter-system linkage testing is the interface list (インターフェース一覧). Confirm system quality across the full data-linkage interaction: whether output data follows the correct naming conventions, data intake timing, error logs at intake, re-intake processing when intake fails, and the storage destination of ingested data.

A key caution is preventing omissions in system settings such as batches. Inter-system linkage testing is often mistaken for a mere data-connectivity check, so master-data preparation tends to be neglected—especially data-linkage batches and error-notification contacts.
システム間連携テストで担保していた基礎的な設定（マスタ等）でも、障害対応や環境切り替えが発生すると設定漏れが起きることがあるため注意が必要である。
システム間連携テストはシステムテストの序盤で実施する。疎通確認のつもりでも、別の機能的問題や運用上の問題に気づくことがある。
テストにはそれぞれ目的がある。システム間連携テストで何を担保するかを理解し、その観点が完了したら次のテストへ進むべきである。序盤実施のため疎通以外の機能障害が副次的に見つかる場合もある。
見つけた課題を今すべて解決しなければならないと勘違いすると、次工程に進めない。どのテストで何を目的にするかを理解し、段階的にシステム品質を上げる考え方が必要である。
見つけた不具合は、早期に別観点の課題を発見できたとポジティブに捉え、課題の位置づけや対処方法をプロジェクトマネージャや業務部門と合意しておけばよい。
システム間連携テストの対象はインターフェース一覧を確認して洗い出す。例: 商品マスタ取り込み（システムA→構築予定システム、更新・新規作成された商品マスタ情報を適宜連携）、処理情報連携（構築予定システム→分析システムB、処理結果を連携）、受注情報取り込み（構築予定システム→システムA、注文情報をリアルタイム連携）。
The 開始・終了判定チェックリスト (start/end judgment checklist) is a tool that enumerates the conditions required to start and end system testing, helping teams make appropriate situational judgments.

Internal SEs are often overwhelmed by WBS-planned tasks plus emerging issues, which makes it hard to calmly decide what must be ready before system test start or what state the system should be in at system test end; this is especially true for first-year internal SEs under the stress and pressure of an unfamiliar project.

Preparing the start/end judgment checklist in advance supports planned preparation and objective assessment of readiness; having the project manager or supervisor review the pre-listed checklist builds confidence to proceed.
Viewpoints to cover are summarized separately for start judgment (Figure 9-7) and end judgment (Figure 9-8); some projects may need to drill down further from these viewpoints.

System test start judgment — previous-process test results: all test scenarios from the previous process must have been executed (digested); any scenarios that could not be executed must have a valid reason.
System test start judgment — defect-fix results: all discovered defects must be resolved, or at least the defects that must be fixed before the next process starts must have their fixes completed.
System test (システムテスト) completion and environment readiness is judged against a structured checklist covering environment setup, governance, tools, resources, and test results (図9-8).
Test environment (テスト環境) must have the application under test fully deployed, required networks prepared, necessary hardware/equipment ready, and required test data prepared.
Test scenarios (シナリオ) must be fully prepared and assigned to responsible personnel; procedures (テスト手順) for executing each scenario must also be ready.
Rules (ルール) for evidence storage locations and progress/issue management tables or tools must be defined, and personnel must understand them.
The testing organization (体制) must be in place, with resource adjustments completed before execution.
Governance for progress, issues, and defects (進捗、課題、不具合) requires defined confirmation/reporting processes, planned meetings, and explanation of those processes to personnel.
Progress and issue-management tools (ツール) must be identified, understood by staff, and fully configured.
Defect-handling resources (リソース) must include a response structure with capacity secured from both the company and the SIer.
Scenario completion (シナリオ消化状況): all test scenarios must be executed; any unexecuted scenario needs a valid reason.
Defect correction (不具合の改修結果): all found defects must be resolved, or at least those that must be fixed before the next phase starts.
Issues (課題): all extracted issues must be reviewed; those that must be solved during system test must be resolved or have a clear path/outlook to resolution.
Acceptance-test handoff (受入テスト準備 / 連携事項): prerequisites and remaining issues must be shared with the business department before acceptance testing begins.
System test end judgment (システムテスト終了判定) is based on environment readiness plus these result criteria, not on execution volume alone.
現新比較テスト (current-vs-new comparison testing) is a test that compares data output by the old system with data output by the new system in order to comprehensively confirm that there are no defects.

現新比較テスト is frequently used in new-system construction and system-refresh projects that take a Fit & Gap approach. It is also effective in Fit to Standard implementations for customer-facing reports that must produce identical output.
現新比較テスト is suitable when the old and new systems produce exactly the same data or reports (example: customer-facing forms/reports).

現新比較テスト is not suitable when the new system fully overhauls business processes and outputs (example: work that required three reports in the old system becomes entirely unnecessary due to automation), or when the old system is so full of defects that it cannot serve as a comparison baseline.
Data comparison and report (帳票) comparison are conducted differently in 現新比較テスト.

For data comparison: use Excel at small scale; at large scale, dump data into a database and mechanically compare old vs. new records using key fields. A simple verification tool may be built to make the test more efficient.
For report comparison: print samples from both old and new systems, summarize the viewpoints to check in a single Excel comparison table, and share that table with testers.

現新比較テスト (current-vs-new comparison testing) requires anticipating differences (差分) in advance: old and new systems may process different numbers of records due to specification or processing-target differences. Without expected-difference cases planned, investigating unexpected diffs consumes effort and delays test progress.

Difference analysis when mismatches occur is high-difficulty work requiring both specification understanding and data analysis, and is typically feasible only for a limited set of people. Sufficient time and specialist resources should be reserved for this analysis.

現新比較テスト often loads all records for a given period and verifies them mechanically. Automated tools may even perform data verification; if those tools themselves are not quality-assured, the test results cannot be trusted.
Report/form (帳票) checking is frequently done manually; resources for that human review must be secured or schedule will slip.

To compare old and new systems, master data and transaction data must be equivalent (データの断面を合わせる). If the old system is still in production, new master records continue to be created during the test window, so the test data snapshot must be deliberately aligned.

Two methods for aligning data snapshots: (1) suppress production operations so no new master registrations occur, enabling a like-for-like comparison; (2) run 現新比較テスト against a frozen past snapshot of master and transaction data rather than the latest live data. Method (2) may be blocked by system settings, but is effective when allowed.
Performance testing (性能テスト) confirms whether a system can normally process the requirements defined in non-functional requirements.
Organizations may treat all of the test types in Figure 9-9 as performance testing, or treat each type as a separate test.
Load testing (負荷テスト): Generate a realistic load and verify operation. Example: simultaneous-connection test by 100 users as defined in non-functional requirements.
Stress testing (ストレステスト): Generate more than the expected load and verify operation. Example: simultaneous access by more than 100 users to test whether operation and error handling work correctly.

Capacity testing (容量テスト): Generate more than the expected load to verify performance and scalability under anticipated future user counts or data volumes. Example: inject more than the expected amount of data and test scalability.
Long-run testing (ロングランテスト): Continuously process for a long time and verify operation. Example: run the system continuously for 3 days.
Deliverables for performance testing are the same as for system testing (performance-specific test scenarios are required).
When system testing and performance testing are performed separately, artifacts created for system testing can be reused.
Some companies or projects include performance viewpoints inside system testing (e.g., first half follows the test-scenario list from page 227; second half is performance testing).
Performance testing verifies performance defined in non-functional requirements; thoroughly understanding the system's required non-functional requirements is the starting point.

A common problem in performance testing is the lack of (or vague) definition of the required performance level. Without a definition, systems may be judged as slow based only on users' subjective sensory impressions. Create performance benchmarks required by the business and obtain agreement from the business department before proceeding.

Performance tests should be conducted in the production environment or an equivalent environment. Differences between production and verification environments can hide potential defects and should be excluded as a risk. Production environments are often connected to customers, so testers must judge whether testing there is feasible.

If performance testing is done too early in the test phase, it may need to be repeated: functional-test defects often lead to application changes, so earlier performance results no longer guarantee the modified specification. Performance testing should wait until defects have largely settled.

If performance testing is left until immediately before release and issues are found, performance improvements may not finish in time and the release may be postponed. Improvements can require fundamental application changes and significant time. For packaged software or SaaS, vendor investigation and patch development typically add long lead times, so timing must be carefully adjusted.
Evidence (エビデンス) in software testing is the records or proof that tests were conducted. It commonly consists of screenshots of screens operated during tests, plus saved output data and reports (帳票).
Screenshots of the screen are the most frequently used form of evidence. Capture both pre-test and post-test screenshots.
Pre-test screenshots are essential: if only post-test screenshots are kept, later review often becomes ambiguous about which screen was used, what data was entered, and what result occurred.
Typical types of evidence include: test procedure documents (テスト手順書), log files, input/output data, data contents, screenshots, reports (帳票), and login-screen captures.
Evidence-acquisition practice: always retain the state immediately before executing a test step as well as the state after, so the full before/after context is preserved.
In system testing, evidence (エビデンス) must record not only results but also the input information used in the test, so that an SIer can easily reproduce and verify defects using the same inputs.

After entering information and running the system, capture screenshots of the actual behavior. If behavior matches expectations, evidence collection is complete; if it differs, use the screenshots as the basis for a defect report.

Evidence volume can become very large; always write the test-procedure scenario number on the evidence itself and name evidence files so they are tied to that scenario number, guaranteeing searchability.

Evidence must be immediately understandable to the recipient. For defects, add callouts or annotations at the unexpected location so the defect can be pinpointed, reproducibility is increased, and response speed is improved.

Typical evidence set for a scenario consists of three screenshots (immediately preceding screen, action screen, post-action screen) plus a file named with the scenario identifier (e.g., IT Test AAA-001.xlsx).

Example annotation practice: on a login-error screenshot, mark the location where the expected error message should appear and note that incorrect credentials were entered, making the discrepancy explicit.
障害 (failure/incident) is an event caused by unexpected external factors, whereas 不具合 (defect/bug) is an event caused by specification deficiencies, configuration errors, or similar internal issues.
Defects found during the testing phase should be viewed positively as opportunities to raise system quality, not with gloom or guilt over 'yet another defect.'
Humans are incomplete, so systems they build cannot be perfect; that incompleteness is why every project includes a testing phase. Find defects and use them to improve quality.
A defect appears as a difference from the assumed specification, so understanding the specification is essential for detecting defects.

Whether a behavior is a defect depends on the spec. Example ①: an email order is received and certain fields display blank — this is as specified if those fields are optional for the customer. Example ②: an email order is received, nothing is read, and an alert fires — this is as specified if the alert is for customers with delayed payments rather than a problem with the order content.
Defects can be detected only when the specification is understood; testers must grasp the spec and rigorously identify differences from it.
Key framing: 不具合のとらえ方 (how to view defects), 不具合の検出例 (examples of detecting defects), and 不具合を検知し報告する (detect and report defects).

During system testing, even when software matches specifications, testers (especially internal/corporate SEs) may feel unease that it will cause operational problems in real business use. These concerns should be shared promptly with the business department rather than kept internal due to guilt over missing them in requirements definition; the discomfort becomes fuel for better future requirements work.

Non-defect issues that are still operationally unacceptable (業務上NG) can and do occur. Treating them as positive early-warning clues helps avoid post-release situations where business processes cannot run.
If additional modification is required, detecting the gap as early as possible creates more calendar time for countermeasures before the release date.

When testing uncovers omitted requirements that need extra development, the change-management process must be followed. Typical flow: create a change request → assess the change → obtain approval from the change-management approver → implement the change → confirm the change → close. Actual procedures are defined by project-specific rules.

First-year internal SEs rarely hold the approval role but may participate in the assessment of change content. Key assessment questions include: What exactly is being requested and what business problem has appeared? How does this differ from the original assumptions? What is the impact of not making the change? What additional time and cost would the change require? Does the change deliver sufficient return on investment? Can the gap be covered by provisional/mixed operations (temporary coexistence of As-Is and To-Be processes during transition)? Why was the request discovered only now (insufficient consensus, insufficient testing, environmental change)? What lessons can be applied to the next project?

Having excellent programmers and project managers is not what is required to clear defects that must be resolved by release. Talent may increase fix speed, but talent alone cannot wipe out all must-fix defects before release.
Defects are found in the order test scenarios are executed. Fixing them in discovery order prevents adjusting which defects must be fixed by release versus which can be deferred until after release.
Investigate the cause of each defect first, then adjust the order of fixes based on business impact (業務に与えるインパクト), not discovery order.
The in-house SE (社内SE) must coordinate defect-handling priority with the business department (業務部門). Without that coordination, the most serious defects cannot be addressed first.

Share defect details with the SIer and request investigation. A common project failure is that the SIer is occupied with a large volume of existing defect work and cannot start investigating newly found defects.
Requesting investigation and setting priority is not enough: without dates, the SIer may implement fixes according to their own convenience. A definite completion date for investigation must be set.
If no deadline is set, work does not progress and progress cannot be followed. Without both a deadline and follow-up, defect-correction speed will not increase.
Core practice for defect handling: investigate the root cause of defects (不具合の根本原因を究明する).
SIer investigations of defects often stop short of root-cause analysis and merely treat the immediate symptom (e.g., labeling a defect as “master-file setting omission” and applying a local fix).

Internal SE (社内SE) should apply why-why analysis (なぜなぜ分析) to the SIer’s stated cause, asking: Why was the defect not found in earlier test phases? Why is it being discovered now? Why was the master file not configured correctly in the first place?

Once a true root cause is identified, conceptual skills—lateral thinking (水平思考) and critical thinking (クリティカルシンキング)—should be used to hypothesize whether similar latent defects exist elsewhere, then to direct the SIer to investigate those related areas.

A typical horizontal-expansion workflow after root-cause identification includes: (1) checking other configuration-change locations, (2) reviewing release-operation procedures, and (3) searching for additional test-coverage gaps.

Possible underlying causes to consider when a master-file setting error surfaces late: a configuration change performed during system test, a mistake in the release procedure, or an earlier-phase test omission.

Figure 9-12 illustrates the defect-deepening loop: SIer report → internal-SE why-why analysis → identified-cause horizontal expansion, with verification of related setting changes, release procedures, and other test leaks.
A system test completion report needs only three simple contents: test progress, test results, and future actions.
The most important factor when creating a system test completion report is whose perspective (audience) it is written for.
Merely summarizing data—how many tests were executed, how many defects were found, and how many remain incomplete—is insufficient; anyone can do that.
A report must understand what the recipient needs and then strip the content down to an appropriate level of abstraction.

Report content should be tailored by audience (Figure 9-13). For a development lead: coverage of system test scenarios; scenario overview; counts of tests, resolved defects, and remaining defects; outlook for remaining-defect fixes and impact on acceptance testing; and future actions toward resolution.
For an IT project manager: counts of tests, resolved defects, and remaining defects; outlook for remaining-defect fixes and impact on acceptance testing; and future actions toward resolution.

For a business project manager: a summary of system test results; outlook for remaining-defect fixes and impact on acceptance testing; and among discovered issues, those that require project-level judgment.
For executives and similar stakeholders: current project status and the impact on the business.

In large-scale projects, a first-year internal SE (社内SE 1年生) almost never reports directly to a project manager or executives; in small-scale projects this can happen, so one must consciously decide who needs to hear what and prepare reports at an appropriate level of granularity.
Early-career internal SEs may rarely present to large audiences, but opportunities for reports and presentations grow with experience and results; not everyone is naturally good at public speaking.

Content comes first when reporting: the goal is not fluent, hesitation-free delivery but proper information sharing. Even a nervous, imperfect explanation can achieve that goal. Delivery matters, but the substance of the report matters more. Senior listeners usually notice nervousness and listen kindly.

Presentation skill is more practice than talent. Even highly skilled presenters rehearse alone (e.g., in an empty meeting room). Solo practice helps; practicing with a colleague who can act as a sounding board is even more effective.

After thorough preparation, hesitate or fear no longer—there is nothing more that can be prepared. Approach the report as if ‘borrowing their chest’ (胸を借りるつもりで). Unexpected questions or critiques are not negative: they raise system quality and grow the reporter. Treat feedback as something to enjoy rather than fear.
Mindset for reporting in front of people (人前で報告するときの心得): prioritize content over smoothness, rehearse, then deliver with composure and treat critique as growth.
Acceptance testing (受入テスト) is the final test conducted immediately before release; it verifies from a business-operations viewpoint whether the new way of working will actually run well.
Internal SEs (社内SE) support the business department in running acceptance tests. This is the last chance to raise system quality before go-live.

If the business department has never run a project, they may need training on testing and help creating scenarios. Even then, only the business department—not the internal SE—must give the final stamp of approval that the system quality is acceptable.
The split between what internal SEs should support and what they should not support must be kept clear; if that boundary is vague, responsibility also becomes vague.

Internal SE SHOULD support: sharing system-test results (including defect-fix status and constraints) and sharing test scenarios; confirming that the application as fixed in system testing is deployed in the acceptance-test environment.
Master-data preparation is mixed (YES/NO): the internal SE can provide a list of which master data is needed for which scenarios, but the actual values must be prepared by the business department.

Even after perfectly executed system testing, issues will still be discovered during acceptance testing (受入テスト). First-year in-house SEs should understand the nature of these findings; they are deliberately called 'issues' (課題) rather than 'bugs/defects' (不具合).

During acceptance testing it is common to realize that the business department’s process considered in requirements definition was insufficient, so the resulting system requirements were also inadequate.

The business department—not the in-house SE—must decide whether to start operations with the current specification or to repair only the absolutely necessary parts before release. Not every raised issue requires immediate investigation by the in-house SE.
Business and technology continually evolve, so a perfect system never exists. A project’s purpose is to contribute to the expected goals within a defined period, not to construct a perfect system.
Acceptance-test scenario (from a business viewpoint): marked NO; these are the test scenarios written from the operational/business perspective.
Basic-operation training: marked YES; this is training on how to operate the new system.
Business-operation training: marked NO; this is training to perform work under the new process. If it is not completed before acceptance testing, test delays become a risk.
Test-implementation organization and environment: marked NO; this covers involving the necessary resources and arranging physical test locations.
Management method (joint implementation): build rules and processes so that issues and defects detected by the business department can be quickly absorbed, reviewed, and repaired.

SIer inquiry-system construction: marked YES; establish the SIer’s organization and shifts so investigation can start immediately when a defect is found, including arranging contact with the SE who wrote the code.

System defects occur due to recognition discrepancies (認識齟齬). Such discrepancies arise most easily between people, between one's own team and other teams, and between one's own company and other companies.
Defects found during testing should be viewed positively as opportunities that raise system quality.
A project exists to contribute to an expected purpose within a defined period; building a perfect system is not the goal and this must always be kept in mind.
Time is the greatest enemy of system testing. Planning is essential in order to make the fullest use of limited time.
Using start- and end-criteria checklists that have been reviewed by the project manager or supervisor allows system testing to proceed with confidence.
Regardless of how much support internal SEs provide, after acceptance testing it is the business department that ultimately certifies that the system's quality is acceptable.
System testing functions as a checkpoint that decides whether the company will accept a system built by an SIer; it therefore forms the bridge from system testing into acceptance testing.

Migration (移行) is the means of arriving at operation of a new mechanism from existing operations and existing systems. Except when launching entirely new businesses or services, a transition from existing work/systems to the new mechanism always occurs.

Migration is frequently neglected and treated as: solely the IT department’s job with no involvement from business units; not important to study; something whose dedicated staff can be omitted under resource shortage; something whose planning time can be cut when requirements definition slips; and therefore insufficient preparation for the actual cut-over is regarded as unavoidable.
New operations cannot start unless the migration barrier is successfully passed. An in-house SE (社内SE) cannot stop at merely executing the technical system migration.
Chapter 10 focuses on designing and executing the change-over to the To-Be state (To-Beへの移り変わりを設計、実行する).
Key questions addressed: What kinds of migration exist and how should roles be divided? What must be prepared for migration and from when? How can a migration rehearsal be run successfully?
Chapter 10 of system development/project management covers migration (移行) from As-Is (current state) through a transitional period (過渡期) to To-Be (future state after migration).
Four elements must be considered together in migration: (1) System/application, (2) Data, (3) Business processes, and (4) Operations and maintenance (運用保守).
Business migration (業務移行) requires designing the transitional period: how work is handed over until the To-Be business flow can actually be executed.
System migration (システム移行) concerns how the application is applied to the production environment, including release design (リリース設計).
Data migration (データ移行) is essential: replacing only the system 'container' without migrating its contents (data) means the new system cannot operate.

Operations handover (運用引き継ぎ) is critical because intended benefits of a system are realized during the operations period; a smooth start of operations/maintenance allows planned effects to be harvested as intended.

Migrating the system alone cannot make a project succeed. Even an excellent system will fail to operate well if: required data is missing, users are not proficient with the new system, or there is no inquiry/support window.

Chapter 10 topics include: migration-related terminology (移行関連用語), migration procedures/steps (移行の段取り), the migration plan document (移行計画書), data migration, improving migration quality (移行品質の向上), the flow of operations handover, and support for business migration (業務移行の支援).
An operations/maintenance handover plan (運用保守 引き継ぎ計画) is part of ensuring operations can be stood up smoothly after go-live.
In system construction projects, four types of migration are required when moving from an old mechanism to a new one: business, system, data, and operations/maintenance.
Migration (移行) means moving from an old mechanism (古い仕組み) to a new mechanism (新しい仕組み).
Business migration (業務移行) is shifting from old business (旧業務) to new business (新業務).
System migration (システム移行) is switching applications from old to new.
Data migration (データ移行) is transferring data from the old system to the new system; if data required by the new system does not exist in the old system, this includes creating that data.

Staged (phased) migration across multiple sites (複数拠点で段階的に移行) is illustrated with locations A and B, each going through old business, migration, new business, hypercare, release, a transition period (過渡期), a migration program (移行プログラム), and operations/maintenance migration (運用保守移行).
Related migration-phase terms include: operations (運用), maintenance (保守), site/location (拠点), hypercare (ハイパーケア), release (リリース), and transition period (過渡期).
移行プログラム (migration program): mechanisms and tools used to migrate data from an old system to a new system.
過渡期 (transition period): the period when old and new mechanisms coexist. Even when old and new systems are mixed, business operations and systems must continue to run normally.
リリース (release): making a constructed service publicly available. Also called カットオーバー (cutover), ローンチ (launch), or サービスイン (service-in).
切り戻し (rollback / cutback): after a release, reverting to the previous state due to some circumstance.
ハイパーケア (hypercare): special support for failures and inquiries immediately after release. A dedicated hypercare organization (臨戦態勢 / battle-ready posture) is built to provide this support.
運用保守移行 (transition to operations and maintenance): after hypercare, handing over operations to the operations and maintenance team.
段階移行 (phased / staged migration): when multiple sites exist, releasing site by site, or releasing by function/module, then migrating.
一括移行 (big-bang / all-at-once migration): migrating everything to the new system at once, regardless of site order or functional split.
並行移行 (parallel migration): running the new system in parallel with the existing system, then switching over after confirming stable operation.
移行計画書 (migration plan document): document that describes the overall plan for migration.
本番移行手順書 (production migration procedure document): procedure document for the actual migration, created by the SIer based on the migration plan.
移行リハーサル手順書 (migration rehearsal procedure document): rehearsal procedure document created from the production migration procedures.

Figure 10-4 compares three release timings: 段階移行 (phased: e.g. site A then site B, old → new), 一括移行 (all sites/functions cut over together), and 並行移行 (old and new run in parallel, then switch after 並行稼働 / parallel operation).

Production migration is pursued by rotating the PDCA cycle (Plan, Do, Check, Action). The steps are: collect information for the migration plan → create the migration plan → prepare for migration → conduct a migration rehearsal → evaluate the migration rehearsal → improve tools and procedures. After migration quality is assured, proceed to production migration.

The starting point of the migration plan is the To-Be business flow, which depicts the future state of business and systems. Work backward from the To-Be business flow to collect information needed for system, data, and business migration.
Information to collect for migration planning includes: requirements definition documents (要件定義書), migration requirements (移行要求), and the system landscape (システムランドスケープ).

Key artifacts in the migration PDCA cycle: migration plan document and production migration procedure document (plan creation); migration environment design document covering tools and data (preparation); migration rehearsal procedure document (rehearsal); production migration procedure document after quality is assured (production cutover).
Migration PDCA mapping: Plan = planning, Do = execution, Check = evaluation, Action = improvement.
Create a migration plan from collected information; requirements often bloat under a 'bigger is better' mindset, so distinguish Nice-to-have from Must and keep only truly necessary requirements.

Do not write the rehearsal procedure first and then derive the production procedure from it—that order is reversed and prevents a true production-migration rehearsal. Write the production migration procedure first; rehearsal exists to validate processes and tools in a near-production form and thereby guarantee production-migration quality.

Prepare data, tools, and other assets for cutover. Migration tools are often omitted from system testing because they are one-off; if their quality is not guaranteed, migrated-data quality is not guaranteed and the new system may fail to run. Include explicit system-test scenarios that exercise the migration tools.

Derive the rehearsal procedure from the production procedure. Account for differences between verification and production environments: drop steps that can be confirmed only in production and add steps that exist only in the verification environment. For steps that still cannot be rehearsed because of environment constraints, allocate extra verification time during the actual production cutover.

After rehearsal, evaluate and improve; confidence in production cutover requires this loop. If one rehearsal does not achieve the needed quality, run two or three more. Isolating poorly executed steps or deficient migration programs and raising their quality separately is also effective.

A migration plan document (移行計画書) must clearly distinguish the scope the in-house SE will execute from the scope they will not execute, and should also describe expectations of business departments and SIers in order to reduce recognition gaps.
Purpose (目的): First clarify whether the document covers migration of business, system, data, or operations/maintenance, then state the goals the migration should achieve.

Prerequisites (前提事項): Record high-level premises of the migration (e.g., this plan covers only system migration while the business department writes the business migration plan; data verification is omitted and left to system testing). Prerequisites are critical and must be agreed among stakeholders.

Migration targets (移行対象): Specify what applications and data move from the old system to the new one. For data, decide not only which items to migrate but how far back historical data goes. In small projects, skipping data migration and re-entering everything by hand can be an option. Confirm necessity and inevitability, then narrow the targets.

Overall migration policy (移行全体方針): State whether migration will be staged, big-bang (一括移行), or parallel (並行移行). When multiple sites are involved, agree the release sequence with stakeholders and document it.
Business migration policy (業務移行方針): Even if IT and business migration plans are written separately, record premises that the business migration depends on, to prevent misunderstandings.
Figure 10-6 is an example of items to include in a migration plan, covering purpose, prerequisites, targets, overall policy, and business-migration policy.

System migration policy documents how applications and system environments will be moved to the new system; existing-system amortization (write-off) is a frequent discussion point, so the policy must state whether the project itself sets the direction or whether that is left to the operations/maintenance team.

Data migration policy should specify the means of migration, the kinds of data to be migrated, volume, and time period, and should also state whether non-migrated data will be cared for. Example: only the most recent five years of data are in-scope for the new system; earlier data is out of scope; the old system is planned to be discarded six months after go-live, so business departments must organize and retain any information they still need.

Role/organization descriptions should not focus solely on work performed by internal SEs; they must also record work that will not be performed internally (i.e., expectations of other parties). Data-migration tasks in particular tend to have an ambiguous boundary between IT-department and business-department work, so explicit alignment is required.

The overall schedule through migration completion must take system testing into account. If system testing will use migrated data, a migration rehearsal must occur before system testing. If rehearsal and system testing are not linked, a separate plan is needed for guaranteeing the quality of the migrated data.

Migration-environment design must clarify in advance its impact on training and testing. Example: if the migration environment is the same as the test/training environment, training cannot occur during the rehearsal window, so schedule adjustments are required.

Operations-and-maintenance transition policy must state the timing and the from/to parties of the handover. When the SIer that developed the new system is different from the SIer that has been operating the existing system, an agreed high-level handover policy and role split are essential; otherwise recognition gaps later appear as extra cost.
The purpose of data migration is not to migrate data beautifully; it is to prepare the data required for new business operations, migrate it, and create a state in which operations can start.

Data migration is carried out through cooperation among multiple parties such as internal SE, business departments, and SIer. Because multiple stakeholders are involved, agreement on role sharing is essential to prevent discrepancies in understanding.
Role sharing in data migration (Figure 10-7): ① preparing the data and ⑤ confirming data quality are not the responsibility of internal SE; they belong to the business department.

How to systematically transport data from the old system to the new system, and guaranteeing the quality of that work, fall within the responsibility of internal SE and SIer (② creating transport tools, ③ transporting the data, ④ guaranteeing work quality).
When transporting data into the new system, combinations of options (as shown in Figure 10-8) must be considered; not everything needs to be solved solely by internal SE or SIer.
If a data source does not exist, it is necessary to consider who will create the data and how, in preparation for the new system's go-live.
Successful data migration requires not only high-quality tools and procedures but also deliberate effort to narrow the migration scope (targets).
Data migration risk is framed as a 2x2 matrix of migration-target size versus migration-preparation quality (Figure 10-9).
Maximum risk occurs when migration targets are large (many data types, high volume, many sites) AND preparation quality is low.
A large target set consumes so much preparation effort that raising quality becomes difficult; therefore narrowing the target set is itself a quality-improvement tactic.
Data migration does not mean moving every existing record into the new system; requirements typically inflate and must be re-anchored to the original purpose.
Four-quadrant risk outcomes: many targets + low quality = large risk; many targets + high quality = medium risk; few targets + low quality = small risk; few targets + high quality = small risk.

Data-migration variations (Figure 10-8) are classified by three axes: (1) data source exists vs. does not exist, (2) transport as-is vs. convert-and-transport, (3) means = Excel-style manual preparation, mechanical migration-tool load, or direct registration into the new system.

The greatest method for raising migration (移行) quality is practice/rehearsal. The more rehearsal done before production, the better the actual migration will go; raising rehearsal quality is equivalent to raising production migration quality.
Migration rehearsal quality depends on how production-like it can be made. This applies not only to procedures, data, and migration tools but also to mindset.
Sports adage that applies equally to migrations: practice as if it were the real event, and treat the real event as if it were practice.
Conducting rehearsal with production-level tension and concentration produces higher-quality rehearsal.
For a first-year in-house SE, the first production migration or release is typically stressful; treating rehearsal as part of production itself can reduce the stress of the actual cutover.
In migration rehearsal, responding to discovered issues is critical. The more issues found, the more fruitful the rehearsal is considered.
Leaving discovered issues unaddressed is absolutely NG.
How to combine rehearsal with the verification process is an important design choice; one option is to plan system tests after the rehearsal.
Effective verification enables discovered issues to be efficiently turned into improvement actions.
Migration rehearsal (移行リハーサル) is conducted for production migration (本番移行), but not everything will match production conditions.
Example of rehearsal–production difference: production may integrate with multiple other systems, while rehearsal may allow linkage with only a limited set of systems.
Understanding differences (差分) between production and rehearsal, and mitigating risks that arise from those differences, is important.

Risk-mitigation tactics include separately planning verification for processes that could not be executed in rehearsal (to guarantee quality) and allowing sufficient migration time for work that can only be done in production.
No matter how meticulously a migration rehearsal is planned, unexpected situations (不測の事態) will occur.

Examples of unexpected situations: transport stoppages that prevent staff from coming on site; a responsible person falling ill and being unable to work; tools not behaving as expected because of master data that exists only in production.
The specific content of unexpected events cannot be predicted, but it is possible (and valuable) to assume that unexpected events will happen.
Anticipating that unexpected situations will occur changes composure when they actually arise; remaining calm and treating them as expected is treated as a mindset issue.
Figure 10-10 (リハーサルから本番移行へ) depicts repeated migration rehearsals, each followed by issue resolution and quality improvement, leading to production migration.

Until hypercare, project team members handle inquiry response and incident/fault handling. After hypercare, once the system has reached a reasonably stable operational state, handover is performed to the existing operations and maintenance team.
Operations handover requires identifying which handover pattern applies and specifying the people with whom communication is needed.
Pattern ①: Handover to an existing operations/maintenance team when development and operations/maintenance are performed by different SIers (SIer A builds the system; SIer B runs operations).
Pattern ②: Handover from the project development team to the company’s own (in-house) operations/maintenance team.
Pattern ③: Handover to an existing operations/maintenance team when the same SIer performs both development and operations/maintenance.
Pattern ④: The development team continues to perform operations and maintenance itself, so no handover to a separate operations team is required.
Typical flow: project development team → system construction → hypercare → operations handover (when needed) → ongoing operations/maintenance.
At project start it is mandatory to agree which team will take over operations and maintenance after system construction; related handover costs must also be estimated in advance.

When the system-construction SIer and the operations/maintenance SIer differ, both knowledge-transfer effort from the construction SIer and the extra effort that will fall on the existing operations SIer must be properly budgeted.

In some cases the development team itself continues to handle operations and maintenance; if this direction is not decided before the project begins, operations-handover budgets cannot be estimated accurately.

Handover to an existing operations team follows these steps: (1) list all handover tasks required to maintain the new system; (2) write procedure manuals for those tasks; (3) estimate effort from the task list; (4) create a handover plan from the tasks and effort; (5) execute the handover; (6) evaluate the handover and formally transfer responsibility.

Handover execution itself has three stages: document reading (understand operations from the manuals, then hands-on training, optionally with a comprehension test); shadowing (observe the project team performing operations during the hypercare period); and actual operations (the receiving team performs the work while the project team monitors, advises and supports).
Even if system-side migration (data, applications, etc.) succeeds, a project cannot succeed unless business/operational transition (業務移行) also succeeds.
Business transition means moving from old business processes and services to new ones that run on the new system.
For internal business applications, users must be trained and must become proficient in the new business processes.
For systems used directly by external customers, customers must be made aware of the new system/service and must become accustomed to using it.
If business transition fails, rollback to the old system is possible even when technical cutover succeeded.
It is a serious mistake to treat business transition as solely the business department’s concern and to focus only on reaching release.
The essential mission of an in-house SE in a business company is supporting achievement of business goals; system construction is only one means to that end.
If business transition fails and the project fails, the in-house SE’s contribution is insufficient no matter how excellent the system itself is.

Forcing a release when business transition is incomplete almost certainly produces a large volume of post-release inquiries, high load on the in-house SE, a prolonged period before stable operations, and delayed handover to the operations/maintenance team.
Key principle: do not treat business transition as someone else’s problem; in-house SEs must actively support it.
Internal SEs (社内SE) must check whether business migration (業務移行) is being promoted, provide appropriate support, and issue alerts to the project when needed.

Key viewpoints for checking business migration (業務移行チェック項目) include: assignment of migration personnel, transitional-period business design, data work, training proficiency, business-migration documentation, and how the internal SE is involved.

移行担当配置: Confirm that responsible persons and role divisions are clearly defined. Without a coordinator for business migration, work that falls between teams (お見合い) tends to occur. Small projects may survive without a dedicated person, but large-scale projects require a dedicated migration promoter (専任の移行推進者).

過渡期の業務設計: Business migration requires designing operations for the transitional period between As-Is and To-Be identified in requirements definition. This is especially mandatory when business applications are introduced to multiple sites in stages.

データ作業: Master data that does not exist in the old system must be created, and data migrated from the old system must be converted into formats usable by the new system. If these man-hours are not included in the business department’s tasks, the internal SE must get them to understand the necessity and adjust schedule and resources.
トレーニング習熟度: Confirm that training is not left as a one-off activity. Training without verification of proficiency has unclear effectiveness.

業務移行ドキュメント: If the business department lacks awareness of documentation, one approach is to include the deliverables expected from the business department in the migration plan so they become visible.
Systems harvest (realize) the intended effects during the operational period; if operations and maintenance start up smoothly, planned effects can be harvested as scheduled.
The purpose of data migration is to prepare the data required for new business operations, migrate it, and create a state in which operations can start.
Until hypercare, project members handle inquiries and incident response; after hypercare, once operations have stabilized to a certain degree, handover to the operations and maintenance team occurs.
In-house SE must not focus only on system migration; migration must consider four aspects: system, data, business operations, and operations/maintenance.
Data migration involves multiple parties (in-house SE, business departments, SIer, etc.), so misunderstandings easily arise; agreement on role division is essential.
The best way to raise migration quality is migration rehearsal; raising the quality of the rehearsal is equivalent to raising the quality of the production migration.
Even if system migration succeeds, without business-process migration an unused mechanism will be created.

A system development project in this book's framework proceeds through: プロジェクト起案 (project proposal), プロジェクト立ち上げ (project kickoff), 要件定義 (requirements definition), 基本設計 (basic design), システムテスト (system testing), 受入テスト (acceptance testing), 移行 (migration), and 運用引き継ぎ (operations handover).
システムリリース (system release) is the last process of a system development project.
From the viewpoint of starting new operations (新業務) or new services (新サービス), system release is not an ending but the point at which you are ready to stand at the starting line.
After release, the constructed system begins to be used and to contribute to the company's business.

A key mindset for system release and operations is that systems are used over many years, improved during that time, and then used further; a modest delay in release is therefore minor relative to the long operational life of the system.
Release delay relative to long-term operations can be compared to the starting line of a 100 km marathon being only a few meters behind the expected position.
First-time system releases often bring anxiety that a poor ending could make all prior work worthless (the reverse of “all’s well that ends well”).
Project members should remain unperturbed by modest troubles and keep composure of mind when entering the final processes of a project (release and operations).
The major flow from system release into actual operations consists of release work, hypercare, and operations/maintenance handover work performed in parallel.
Chapter 11 assumes SIer support and that operations/maintenance will be handed over to an existing operations/maintenance team.
Decision (judgment) points should be established for system release and operations handover.

Key actors and activities in the release-to-operations flow include the business department, internal SE, SIer, migration rehearsal, release work, hypercare, operations/maintenance, and business improvement.
The operations/maintenance team is involved in handover, training, ongoing operations/maintenance, and operations improvement.
Four judgment/measurement points in the flow: (1) release decision, (2) stable-operation decision, (3) operations-handover decision, and (4) effect measurement.
The release-to-operations sequence spans from Chapter 10 (including migration rehearsal and release) into Chapter 11 (hypercare, handover, and operations).

In the process leading to system release and operations handover, four main judgment (decision) points should be established: (1) release judgment, (2) stable operation judgment, (3) operations handover judgment, and (4) effect measurement. These points may also be called judgment meetings depending on the organization.

Release judgment (リリース判断): Before commencing the actual release, confirm that prior testing and migration rehearsals have completed without problems and that preparations for release work are in place. Obtain a GO sign at this point before proceeding with the work.

Stable operation judgment (安定稼働判断): After all release work is finished and operational confirmation is complete, decide whether production operations can begin. Production operations start only when both the business department and the IT department give an OK.

Operations handover judgment (運用引き継ぎ判断): After release, the project team continues to handle incidents and inquiries for a period. Once a sufficient level of stable operation is confirmed, handover occurs to the existing operations and maintenance team. When on-site hypercare is being performed, this judgment can also serve as the on-site withdrawal decision. Handover is required for both the IT department and the business department (to their respective existing ops/maintenance teams); the timing of handover need not be the same for both sides.

Effect measurement (効果測定): Targeted effects should be observed and evaluated periodically rather than treating release as the end of the effort. Compare actual results against the original assumptions and use the gaps to identify seeds for improvement. New systems and new business processes are not finished simply because they have been released.

After operations have been handed over, ongoing operations maintenance and operations improvement (運用保守、運用改善) are performed by the operations team to achieve lower-cost operations through continuous process and system improvement. Effect measurement (point ④) is performed against the original project goals and is conceptually separate from post-handover operations improvement.
Before moving to release work, a release judgment (リリース判断) is performed to confirm that preparations are sufficiently complete.

Depending on the company, creating release judgment documents such as a release judgment criteria document (リリース判定基準書), release checklist (リリースチェックリスト), or migration judgment document (移行判定書), and/or participating in judgment meetings (判定会), may be required.
The purpose of all such documents and meetings is the same: for the appropriate roles or meeting bodies to determine that release preparation is complete.

Release judgment confirms that preparations are in place to start business operations and services with the new system; therefore an in-house SE (社内SE) must not discuss the matter from an IT perspective alone.
Some companies separate IT-department system release judgment from project judgment in a two-stage process, so the company's own judgment process must be confirmed.

Release judgment documents (リリース判定資料) should include, among other items, 承認希望内容 (content requesting approval): at the beginning and end, concisely state what you want approved. Judges handle many projects, so clearly identify which project and which part of the release is being judged (e.g., if there are multiple sites, specify that this judgment is only for the first site).

Release judgment materials should include a project overview describing the targeted business goals and how both business process construction and system construction were carried out as the means to achieve them.

Document project progress by stating how far the project phases have been completed, confirming that all required phases are finished before facing the release decision; if incomplete work remains, prepare explanations of due dates or why remaining work poses no risk.

Record training status to show that training for the new operations has been completed without problems and that operational start is ready; also include progress of any required notifications to customers or business partners.

Summarize test results simply: what tests were performed, number of scenarios, defects found, and remaining defects. Do not explain every test scenario in detail; focus only on points that need to be reported so the intended message is clearly conveyed.

For defect correction status, state the number of defects that occurred and the number resolved. If all defects are fixed, add a brief trend analysis. If unresolved defects remain at the release decision, describe each defect’s overview, its business impact, and the planned fix date.
Coordinate in advance with stakeholders on the release organization (staffing) and emergency contact methods, and document them in the materials.

Include the release schedule covering the flow of work until go-live and the timing of subsequent status reports. For lengthy release work, establish regular checkpoints for confirmation and reporting so that progress remains visible to all related parties.

Present risks so that decision-makers can judge whether to proceed with release while understanding those risks or to consider additional countermeasures; postponement of release is sometimes the correct decision. Never allow known latent risks to remain undisclosed, obtain approval, and then have those risks materialize at the moment of release.

When creating release judgment materials, strongly reuse previously approved judgment documents from the same company, because the same decision-makers typically review them and past materials already incorporate the viewpoints those reviewers care about.

Once a production release is approved in the release-judgment process, no further technical work (testing, data checks, etc.) remains; effort shifts to administrative preparation for post-release hypercare and to the team's mental and physical readiness.
Hypercare (ハイパーケア) is the intensive post-go-live support period; environment and operating-model preparation for it should be completed before release.

War Room (ウォールーム / 作戦室): a dedicated physical or virtual space so that system failures detected after release can be handled immediately. Common patterns are gathering stakeholders in one conference room, or keeping a constant Microsoft Teams link with the SIer's room for rapid information sharing.
Issue-management tools: prepare (or reuse from system testing) a tool that can track incidents and inquiries during hypercare.
Hypercare organization: roles and staffing must be explicit; shift tables (シフト表) are especially useful immediately before and after go-live.
Standing meetings: morning (朝会) and evening (夕会) checkpoints during hypercare to review incidents and status.
Emergency contacts: communication channels and contact lists must be ready for urgent situations.

A first production release is inherently tense and stressful; residual anxiety after all preparations are finished is normal. Mental framing of how to experience and get through the release is part of the work.
Treat the release itself as a learning opportunity (リリースを学びの場にする) rather than only as a risk event.

If a system release fails, follow established procedures, make the appropriate judgment, and execute a rollback (切り戻し). A rollback simply extends current operations for a short additional period rather than creating a catastrophe.
