One or two failed releases typically cost no more than extra payments to the SIer (System Integrator). For a first-year in-house SE (社内SE), both success and failure constitute valuable growth experience.
Physical fatigue accumulated during the pre-release push often causes mental restlessness. Recovering physically frequently allows the mind to settle naturally.
When no further pre-release tasks remain, performing post-release preparations (such as organizing documents) occupies the hands, creates mental leeway, and reduces anxiety.
Block the schedule after release so that time is reserved exclusively for incident (障害) and inquiry handling; avoid inserting meetings for other projects. Time leeway directly produces mental leeway.

High-pressure release situations reveal people's true nature and therefore serve as an excellent learning environment. Observe how seniors and SIers behave under tension: adopt calm, polite responses as models and treat unreasonable behavior as a negative example for personal growth.

First-year in-house SEs (社内SE) must understand two facts about system release: (1) no matter how much training and testing is done, incidents such as failures and inquiries will occur after release to some degree; (2) a hypercare (ハイパーケア) structure must be in place to respond to those incidents quickly.
Hypercare exists because post-release incidents are expected as normal. If zero failures after release were the default, hypercare would not be needed.

During hypercare the atmosphere is tense. Regardless of the cause of a discovered failure, do not fight team members. The opponent to fight is the incident itself, not the business department or the SIer; those stakeholders are allies.

The worst situation to avoid is a user-department-detected failure that never reaches the in-house SE, delaying response and widening the damage. A process must be built to rapidly collect incident information.

Before hypercare, train everyone on the incident-management tool and align with the business department and SIer on the viewpoints and granularity to record: occurrence datetime, impact scope, business impact, severity/importance, and similar attributes.
When responding to incidents, define clear priorities and a process for assigning them; otherwise, handling incidents strictly in arrival order can delay work on major failures and expand damage.
Even during hypercare (臨戦態勢), experts cannot all be on standby at all times; a reliable communication line/contact system must be built so they can be reached when needed.
Do not let internal SEs separately query each SIer incident handler; unify the SIer contact window for receiving and confirming incident reports so information is centralized.
Users experience high stress from work-process change, especially on the first day of a new way of working; system failures amplify that frustration.
On high-stress system-release days, internal SEs must stay calm even if users report incidents emotionally.

Cool-down questions for the internal SE: What is this failure’s impact on the company’s business? Is it limited to some functions or system-wide? Can it be temporarily avoided with provisional operations? Has it been escalated to the appropriate department or team?
System release is only the starting line for new operations or services, not the finish line.
If a serious incident is found during the release window that severely impacts business units or customers, rollback (切り戻し) should be chosen.
Rollback is not failure. True failure is when ideas are proposed but never become projects and remain unimplemented. Reaching release is already major progress.
Even after rollback, fixing issues and preparing a re-release still allows harvesting the planned benefits; prior preparation is not wasted.

Rollback decisions must be driven by business impact, not only technical severity. Example: rollback if an unspecified number of customers are harmed; do not necessarily rollback if a systemically serious defect affects a function unused until month-end and there is time to patch.
Rollback judgment should consider business impact and be made in consultation with the project owner/responsible person.
Some projects skip rollback rehearsals because they reuse migration-rehearsal data for system testing and want to avoid extra effort if they later roll back. This is a mistake.
Preparedness is required: rollback cannot be executed reliably without practice. Rollback must be included in the rehearsal scope.
Key framing: prepare for system rollback (システムの切り戻しに備える); plan and execute rollback with explicit points of attention.

Rollback (切り戻し) judgment points must be made explicit. Rollback itself can take substantial time, so calculate the time required via rehearsals and add that duration into the judgment deadline so the organization can still run on the old system with enough margin.
A common misconception is that IT decides whether to roll back. The project owner (プロジェクト責任者) must decide, because they must judge business impact of the issues and whether to accept rollback risk.

Example: During release, an incident is found where a new feature cannot be provided in some regions. If that region is a strategically important business area, rollback is chosen. If the region has low strategic priority and limited impact, the release may still proceed.

Even with a prepared rollback plan, most people treat actual rollback as a complete surprise (寝耳に水) and do not expect it to be executed. Execution therefore causes confusion, and information sharing is easily forgotten. After rollback, thoroughly notify business departments that the old system and processes will be used, to prevent secondary damage.
There is no time to remain discouraged after a rollback. Switch mindset immediately, perform 5-Whys analysis (なぜなぜ分析) on the causing event, identify root causes, and start work toward re-release.
After release, end project-team hypercare and hand over to the operations/maintenance team once issues have surfaced for a period and both the system and business operations have stabilized.
Do not hand over until the Figure 11-5 checklist confirms the ops/maintenance team can take over without problems.

Incident status: hand over only when the system is running stably and incident volume is trending down. Handing over while the system is unstable and incidents are still rising forces continued developer support, extra communication, and slower response.
Remaining defects (残障害) are as important as incidents. Even if incidents are decreasing, unresolved remaining defects still require development-team work, so they must be progressing before handover.
Handover-destination resources: confirm the receiving team has secured capacity and can actually operate the system. Coordinate in advance so the transfer is not a one-sided dump.
Handover-destination training: confirm the receiving team has completed enough training to run operations and is ready.
Notify stakeholders that after operational handover the inquiry flow changes from the temporary incident-response process to the permanent process.
Other preparations: update incident-management-tool access rights and settings, document access rights, and similar items as part of the handover.
Key terms: ハイパーケア (hypercare), 運用保守チーム (operations/maintenance team), 運用引き継ぎ (operational handover), インシデント (incidents), 残障害 (remaining defects).
When handing over a project, transfer expected operation and maintenance (運用保守) costs to the receiving department if needed, following the company's own rules and procedures.

Handover documents created by project members are usually insufficient as-is: long-involved members omit countless 'obvious' premises and assumed knowledge. Documents must be reviewed from the receiving side's perspective to ensure enough information for actual operational handover.

Development and operations teams often fail to communicate during handover preparation. Conscious, regular information exchange is required so that documentation and handover work are not left until the last minute.

A system does not contribute to the business merely by being built; it delivers value only when used over the long term. Smooth collaboration between development and operations is therefore essential.
Hypercare is typically time-boxed (e.g., two weeks). A common failure is forcing the handover simply because the period ended, even if handover work is incomplete.

A time guideline for handover is useful, but it is more important to verify that the planned handover tasks were actually completed and to decide whether handover can proceed based on that check, not on the calendar alone.
Handover pitfalls should be examined from both the transferring (project) side and the receiving (operations) side.
At project completion there are two kinds of retrospectives (振り返り): a whole-project retrospective and a personal retrospective.

The whole-project retrospective verifies whether the problem the project set out to solve was actually solved. This is a critical task because operations and services continue, and improvement continues as long as it is cost-effective; you must know how far you have currently reached.

Project retrospectives are often compiled and distributed as reports by the project manager. A first-year in-house SE (社内SE 1年生) is rarely directly involved, but should still analyze and reflect on the project themselves before reading the report.

Doing your own analysis first lets you compare your viewpoint and evaluation with those of the project manager and seniors. Gaps in perspective suggest seeing and thinking from a higher vantage point and help you acquire one facet of conceptual skill: a multifaceted viewpoint (コンセプチュアルスキルの多面的視野).

The personal retrospective asks whether you performed the role you were assigned as expected. You identify issues and things that did not go well and turn them into action plans so you can improve on the next project.

Holding interviews with the project manager, your supervisor, and counterparts in the business department is effective because you can borrow others’ viewpoints to recognize your own contributions and issues.

When reflecting on a project, use the viewpoints in Figure 11-6. Viewpoints you were personally involved in become personal reflection; viewpoints you were not involved in become project-level reflection.
It is best to reflect on all listed viewpoints. Certain viewpoints (underlined in the original figure) are especially recommended for first-year in-house SEs (社内SE 1年生).

Reflection (振り返り) is effective for accelerating growth (as explained on page 57). Most people work hard on projects, but almost no one works hard on reflection. People who want to grow quickly and raise their skill level should deliberately do retrospectives.
Project retrospective viewpoints (プロジェクト振り返りの観点, Figure 11-6) are grouped into several lenses, including project measures/policy (施策観点), project management (管理観点), IT, and business (業務観点).

Project measures / management related items include: resource management (リソース管理), budget management (予算管理), risk management (リスク管理), vendor management (ベンダー管理), progress management (進捗管理), scope management (スコープ管理), and expectation management (期待値管理).

IT-related retrospective items include: solution selection (ソリューション選定), team composition (チーム編成), deliverable management (成果物管理), SIer selection (SIer選定), development methodology (開発手法), development management (開発管理), and organizing system requirements (システム要件の整理).

Business-related retrospective items include: strategy (戦略), cost-effectiveness (費用対効果), aim of the plan (企画の狙い), business contribution (ビジネス貢献), business design (業務設計), training (トレーニング), involving stakeholders (関係者の巻き込み), and organizing business requirements (業務要件の整理).
Even incidents during hypercare should be treated as opportunities to raise quality; do not fight business departments or SIers—fight the incidents themselves.
After system release, perform hypercare until stable operation; hand over to the operations/maintenance team only after incidents have largely surfaced.

Recommended retrospective viewpoints for first-year in-house SEs: strategy, planning intent, cost-effectiveness, business contribution, progress management, organizing system requirements, business design, and organizing business requirements.
Incidents of various sizes after system release are normal; hypercare structures exist for this reason—do not become unnecessarily nervous.
Rollback (切り戻し) is not failure; treat it as a postponed release, regroup, and try again.
Project-completion retrospectives have two types—overall project and individual; doing both accelerates growth.
System release is the last project process, but from the viewpoint of new business or new services it is standing at the starting line.
